articles.title: Google Pixel 11 Specs Leak Ahead of Next Month’s Unveiling
articles.summary: Early leaks for the Google Pixel 11, Pro, and Pro Fold reveal potential specs, a variety of new colors, and a price increase across the lineup.
articles.body:
Google is set to reveal its Pixel 11 lineup on August 12th, and thanks to recent leaks, the company may have little new to tell about its coming smartphones .

For instance, a 9to5Google report this week covered "three [Amazon] listings that appear to be placeholders" published early, "with official images in tow." The listings, the outlet wrote, revealed the Pixel 11 in many colors with descriptions labeling them "Midnight," "Fuchsia," and "Moss." Also, the Pixel 11 Pro was listed in "Dune," "Light Fog," and "Pine." The Pixel 11 Pro Fold was there, too, in Midnight and Pine. According to that leak, the Pixel 11 will have a 6.3-inch display, 256GB SSD, 12GB of RAM, a 4,985mAh battery, and will start at $899, or a hundred bucks higher than the Google Pixel 10 launched at.

The next day, Android Authority reported that it had seen yet more screenshots of the listings, and that these confirmed the phone would have a 120Hz refresh rate, a 13MP front camera, and would sport Bluetooth 6 and Wi-Fi 6E capability. Interestingly, the outlet wrote that the base Pixel 11 will have a "2,856 x 1,280 resolution," conflicting with the 1,080 x 2,424 that 9to5Google reported. (I don't see that in the screenshots Android Authority published, and, as usual, it's best to take these leaked specs with a grain of salt.)

Moving on, Android Authority also writes that screenshots showed the Pixel 11 Pro with the same display size as the Pixel 11, a 13MP front camera, and be capable of 120x digital zoom, and will cost between $1,099 and $1,449, up from $999 to $1,399 for last year's model. The article says the Pro XL will get a 6.8-inch, 120Hz display with a 2,991 x 1,344 resolution, feature a 5,115mAh battery, and a 13MP front camera. Like the base Pixel 11, it will apparently support Bluetooth 6 and Wi-Fi 6E. Citing Droid Life, Android Authority says the 11 Pro XL's pricing could range from $1,299 to $1,649, a $100 bump from its predecessor.

Lastly, the Pixel 11 Pro Fold may have a 6.5-inch, 120Hz outer OLED display with a 2,342 x 1,080 resolution. It'll also have a 4,750mAh battery, 13MP front camera, and will support Bluetooth 6 and Wi-Fi 6E, according to the leak. It may be priced at $1,899 (up from last year's $1,799 base model) for the 256GB version, and $2,019 for the 512GB option. The author noted that the 10 Pro Fold had a larger, 5,015mAh battery pack and speculated that the smaller capacity in these screenshots could be inaccurate placeholder text. Of course, so could anything else in the early, now-deleted listings.

One thing that is for sure is that there will be a little color-shifting, glowing orb tucked into the Pixel 11's camera bar. 9to5Google noticed that in the animation that plays on Google's teaser page for the forthcoming phone. What it represents is up for debate, but let's have a little fun and speculate that it has something to do with AI.

Say it with me one last time: besides that glowing orb from Google's actual website, any number of the specs from these leaks could be wrong, and we will know for sure what's going on with these phones in just a little less than a month, when Google reveals the phones for real.

Wes is a freelance writer (Freelance Wes, they call him) who has covered technology, gaming, and entertainment steadily since 2020 at Gizmodo, Tom's Hardware, Hardcore Gamer, and most recently, The Verge. Inside of him there are two wolves: one that thinks it wouldn't be so bad to start collecting game consoles again, and the other who also thinks this, but more strongly.

articles.title: MSI's Newest QD-OLED Gaming Monitor Is an Absolute Speed Demon With Breathtaking Visuals
articles.summary: The MSI MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 delivers stunning visuals and exceptional speed in a 360Hz ultra-wide monitor package.
articles.body:
MSI is continuing its push into high-quality QD-OLED gaming monitors with the MSI MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36. At $899, it serves as a true successor to one the MSI MPG 341CQPX QD-OLED I tested in late 2024. It comes with some upgrades to the design, extra features, and an updated panel that just gives you more of a great thing while still fitting right into that 34-inch, 3440x1440 ultra-wide curved screen format. With the latest tech and a competitive price, it’s worth a look next to earlier favorites like the Acer Predator X34 OLED or Samsung Odyssey G8 , and it can go head to head with the new Alienware AW3426DW .

MSI MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 – Hands-on Photos

MSI MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 – Design and Features

Like the MSI MPG 341CQPX QD-OLED before it, the MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 features a large, 34-inch ultra-wide display with a 3,440x1,440 resolution and a gentle 1800R curve that boosts immersion a touch without looking too funky for regular use. MSI has refined the design a bit, shrinking down the chin below the display and adding a special sensor, but otherwise it’s not so different. The monitor still has a basic RGB-lit segment on the back that adds little to the tame overall design, an easy-to-use five-way joystick for controls, and a power and shortcut button beside the joystick. The latter button annoyingly still defaults to launching MSI Intelligence Center (which tries to install itself automatically over USB or DisplayPort) and can’t be customized to do anything else without the app installed.

One smart change MSI made was in the stand. Rather than the wide-legged base of the earlier model, the MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 includes a flat, hexagonal base that doesn’t dominate so much desk space. Though it would seem less supportive at first, the stand is heavy enough in comparison to the monitor that it holds steady even while I make adjustments to the screen position. The stand supports a pretty typical range of movements with a 20-degree vertical tilt range, a 60-degree swivel range and 110mm of height adjustment. It has just a little pivot, but since the monitor is wider than the stand is tall, you can’t plan on pivoting it 90 degrees for a vertical setup. If you don’t like the stand, you can swap to 100x100mm VESA mounting. The stand has a convenient cable-routing hole in the middle to tidy things up, though it’s too small to support every cable if you filled every port on the monitor.

On the underside of the MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36, you’ll find two HDMI 2.1 ports and a DisplayPort 2.1a port that all support the full resolution and refresh rate of the monitor. Alongside the DisplayPort and HDMI inputs, the MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 has some USB ports that prove highly useful. There are two USB-A ports that can link back to a desktop with a USB-B backhaul or link to a full-featured USB-C port. That USB-C port is a rockstart, supporting the full display resolution and 360Hz refresh rate while also providing up to 98 watts of power delivery. That’s incredibly handy if you ever use the monitor with a laptop. The monitor also includes a 3.5mm jack for audio output, but it doesn’t have any speakers of its own.

Just below the display is a sensor that can enable a handful of extra features. The monitor can automatically turn off the screen to conserve energy and protect the panel when you step away, and it can wake back up when you return (though it takes a few seconds to start back up). It can also automatically adjust the brightness and other settings based on ambient conditions. With all of these enabled, I found the monitor a little tedious to use, with it adjusting the picture too much and the boot-up taking a little too long for my taste, but these can be dialed in to work with the way you use a monitor. One setting could simply dim the display when I wasn’t looking at it seemingly based on eye sensing, and this seemed perfectly practical.

The MSI MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 performs wonderfully in testing. By default, it runs at 70% brightness with Eco settings and an ultra-low power mode, but this still allows it to hit 205.9 nits with 100% coverage of the sRGB color space and 98% coverage of the DCI-P3 color space. The color accuracy is also impressive in this setting, with a dE Max of 2.02. Dialing up the settings to 100 percent brightness sees the display reach 308 nits while maintaining its color gamut and comfortable 6600K white point. Color accuracy dips a little, but the display still hits an average dE1976 of 1.17 and a max dE1976 of 2.21. It may not be perfect for color critical work like photo and video editing, but it won’t be far off the mark either.

As the MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 has an OLED panel, it naturally has infinite contrast. It also enjoys very fast pixel response times. When the display is set to 360Hz, I can’t see any ghosting in Blur Busters’ UFO test.

HDR settings give the MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 even more means to impress. I measured a peak white point of 366 nits for a full screen window and 603 nits for a 10% window using the True Black 500 HDR setting. With the Peak 1000 setting, the fullscreen and 10% windows didn’t change by more than a few nits, but I measured as high as 1,551 nits for a small highlight comprising less than 4% of the screen area and 900 nits for a window less than 9% of the screen area. Combine these dazzling highlights with the deep black levels, and you get remarkable visuals.

MSI MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 – Gaming and Performance

Gaming on the MSI MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 is a joy. The ultra-wide, 21:9 format gives games an extra level of immersion, by filling that much more of my field of view while the 3440x1440 resolution remains a lot easier for gaming hardware to handle than 4K. That’s important, because the MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 runs at up to 360Hz and supports variable refresh rates to help ensure every frame is delivered in full and screen tearing never crops up.

In practice, it delivers on that promise. 007 First Light was all the more cinematic on the wide-screen, and though it took DLSS and multi-frame generation to even come close to scratching that 360Hz ceiling, the game appeared buttery smooth, helping me dash through the higher-octane action sequences of the game with ease.

The rich contrast and bold color really help present the moody, dark scenes and explosive firefights of 007 First Light well. And the 360Hz refresh rate and ultra-fast pixel response time of the OLED panel make snapping to targets much easier as there’s basically no blurring to impede me. All that speed became even more beneficial in fast-paced games like Trepang2, helping me zip through levels and put the moves on enemies that never knew what hit them.

The display can still have some trouble with glare, which spreads out wide thanks to the curve of the monitor, but the panel has a new coating that helps keep reflected light a bit darker than MSI’s prior monitors. As long as you’re not fighting with strong direct lighting or sunlight, it’ll be pretty great looking. In my office, with overhead lighting on and some daylight trickling into the space, the screen treatment was enough to make reflections very hard to see even on a completely black screen.

Another improvement the MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36 brings is a RGB stripe sub-pixel layout. Early OLED monitors suffer from uncommon subpixel layouts that create issues in fine details, especially text. This presents as color fringing, which can be very distracting. On the MPG 341CQR QD-OLED X36, that issue is gone. It had already been largely solved in the earlier MSI MPG 341CQPX QD-OLED, but here it’s not even a risk.

Mark Knapp is a contributing freelancer for IGN covering everything electronics and gaming hardware. He has over 10 years of experience in the tech industry with bylines at PCMag, Reviewed, CNET, and more. Find Mark on Twitter @Techn0Mark or BlueSky at @Techn0Mark .

articles.title: Critics of Sony's Decision to Kill Physical Discs Call on Gamers to Boycott PlayStation for a Week Next Month, but Will Anyone Listen?
articles.summary: Backers of physical media have called on gamers to boycott PlayStation for a week in August to send a message to Sony that its decision to kill discs from 2028 is unacceptable.
articles.body:
Backers of physical media have called on gamers to boycott PlayStation for a week in August to send a message to Sony that its decision to kill discs from 2028 is unacceptable.

The Does it play? X / Twitter account , which is a fierce critic of Sony’s plan to do away with PlayStation game discs, issued a call to arms that has been viewed on the social media platform nearly 1 million times.

“Sony wants to abandon fans? Let's give them a small taste of their own medicine!” the Twitter account said. “Together with other creators we call for a 1 week #PSBlackout in August. No logins, no play sessions, no purchases on any of Sony's platforms.”

The 100 Best PlayStation Games of All Time

Sony’s rationale for ditching discs is that it’s simply following consumer trends. “In response to shifting trends in consumer preference, new games will be released on PlayStation Store and at retailers in digital formats only,” Sid Shuman, Senior Director, Sony Interactive Entertainment Content Communications, said in a post on PlayStation Blog .

“As consumer preferences and the broader entertainment industry continue to shift away from physical discs to digital, physical game disc production for all new games releasing on PlayStation consoles will be discontinued starting January 2028. Following this date, new games will be available on PlayStation Store and at retailers in digital formats only. This transition has no impact on games that already released, or will be releasing, prior to January 2028 in disc format.

“This is a natural direction for Sony Interactive Entertainment to adapt to consumer trends as the general preference for digital media significantly outpaces physical discs. This transition will enable us to align more closely with how most of our community prefers to access and play games today."

Reinforcing this trend, Mat Piscatella, Senior Director and Video Game Industry Advisor at Circana, said that just seven PlayStation video games had sold more than 100,000 physical units so far this year in the U.S. . Only two PlayStation video games sold more than 10,000 physical units in the U.S. during the week ending July 11.

However, since the announcement, gamers have called on Sony to U-turn on its decision, signing online petitions and swarming over PlayStation social media posts to express concern about video game preservation and ownership — even overshadowing the release of new games that have nothing to do with what’s going on at Sony.

Complaints have also come from other groups. The UK’s Digital Entertainment and Retail Association (ERA) called Sony’s decision “a triumph of corporate convenience over consumer choice.”

In a statement published online , Kim Bayley, CEO of ERA, said its data shows that 25% of under 25s use discs for gaming, and that discs should remain as a choice on top of digital.

“Every year, millions of gamers still choose to buy physical copies because they value true ownership. A disc can be shared with family, traded in, collected, preserved and, crucially, still played years from now. A download licence often offers none of those freedoms,” Bayley said.

Does it play? and other critics of Sony have remained determined to continue the fight. Here’s the boycott statement in full:

If history has told us anything, it’s that video game boycotts rarely result in the action they desire. It probably doesn’t help that Metal Gear Solid 4 will finally escape PS3 prison via Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2 that week. There are of course instances of companies reversing decisions amid a backlash, but, analysts have told IGN , it remains unlikely that Sony will U-turn on this.

Dr. Serkan Toto, CEO of Japanese game industry consultancy firm Kantan Games, suggested that even if half a million people cancelled their PlayStation Plus subscription in protest, it would be just a drop in the ocean for Sony.

"I sympathize with physical media fans, but Sony will not reverse this decision," Toto told IGN. "They of course knew what the online reaction would look like, and they now wait for this storm to pass.

"Sony has over 120 million active PlayStation users," he continued. "Around 50 million people subscribe to PlayStation Plus. As a thought experiment, let's say 500,000 cancel in protest, that would be just 1% of that business gone — of course not enough for Sony to start rethinking. Digital is just too lucrative."

Piers Harding-Rolls, games industry analyst at Ampere, has said a lot has changed over the course of the last two generations. "Console gaming is the last hold-out for physical media in the gaming sector, but physical product has been declining in importance," he said in a post on the Ampere website . "Back in 2013 when the PS4 launched, Ampere data shows that only 13% of total full games unit sales for Sony consoles were digital (including digital-only games). Fast forward to 2025, and this digital share of full game purchases stood at almost 80% of the total.

"Inevitably there will be concerns from PlayStation gamers around various aspects of this announcement including choice, accessing older physical games on new consoles, the ability to collect physical games, and game preservation, however the purchasing trends of gamers are clear."

One analyst said fans of physical media had their chance and blew it, so there’s no going back. “If gamers and preservationists had bought more physical games, Sony wouldn’t have seen the digital sales ratios that justify this decision,” Robin Zhu, a games analyst at Bernstein, told the Financial Times .

For Sony, going all-digital for new game releases will earn it more money from every sale at a time when console sales are expected to plummet due to their rising cost. For a first-party PlayStation game such as The Last of Us, Sony will only keep around 65% of the money from a physical copy, with around 30% going to the retailer and roughly another 5% on manufacturing costs. Meanwhile, for a physical copy of a third-party game such as the Activision-published Call of Duty, Sony will get a licensing fee, likely around 15%.

For downloads, however, the margins are much higher. For a first-party game sold via Sony's own PlayStation Store, the company obviously keeps 100% of the revenue. For third-party games such as Call of Duty, meanwhile, Sony keeps a 30% cut (so, roughly $21 for a $70 game).

Photo by Nikos Pekiaridis/NurPhoto via Getty Images.

Wesley is Director, News at IGN. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.

articles.title: The Best Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Cases You Can Get Today
articles.body:
Another year, another Galaxy Z Fold phone . The eighth iteration, if you can believe it. And actually, it’s not just one, but two phones this time: the same-as-it-ever-was Z Fold 8 Ultra that looks just like the Z Fold 7 , and the wider, passport-style Z Fold 8.

Before you pick a case for one of these phones, decide how much you want to compromise the look and feel of your phone, versus how much you want to protect it. As someone who sits at a desk all day, I like a slim case if I’m using one at all, despite what the chunky ESR clear case currently on my iPhone 15 Pro says. In my service industry days, I preferred something more protective, especially for something as damage-prone as a foldable.

Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Hybrid Shield Magnet Case

Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra Case (Official)

Phone makers don’t usually know for certain the precise dimensions and materials of a phone before it’s released, so my general recommendation is go with first-party cases, if you can afford it. Also, since these are brand new phones, keep in mind that this guide – like any others you encounter right as a phone has been released – is based on past experience with phone cases. For me, that’s about 17 years of slapping plastic, rubber and leather on my phones.

Check out the best Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra cases.

How to Pick a Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Case

Your first consideration when picking a case for your phone is to figure out what you want out of it. Are you looking for something slender to protect the phone from scratches? Something purely aesthetic to express yourself? Is it full-blown protection, in-hand comfort be damned?

Next, pick your ideal price range and line up your options. Look first for long-established brands, and if none of those have what you’re looking for, feel free to expand to those that haven’t been around as long. It’s hard to find case reviews these days, but cases have also just generally gotten better over the years, in my experience. Still, foldables remain a relatively young category, so it’s a good idea to find a reviewer whose tendencies jive with your own. I look for commentary about fit and hand-feel: does it want to pop off easily? Is it too hard to remove? Will it slip out of my hand? That sort of thing.

Finally, don’t forget that these are brand new phones and that case makers don’t all get advance information that lets them make a precise fit. Some brands are good about that, and will ship you a replacement as soon as they’re dialed in later. If you’re committed to a third-party option, make sure they at least offer that. Otherwise, if you know you’re clumsy or you just want a guarantee, go with a phone case that’s made, or at least approved, by Samsung itself.

1. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Hybrid Shield Magnet Case

Samsung’s official Galaxy Z Fold 8 case is usually your best bet right out of the gate, and that’ll be especially true in a year when the company has totally overhauled the physical dimensions of its mainstay foldable. Sure, there have been plenty of leaks that have let case makers generate products based on the actual dimensions of the phone, but without the real thing, they can’t truly test them.

The Hybrid Shield Magnet Case features a split-hinge-cover only thing is that first-party cases are pretty much always pricier than third-party options, and that’s true here, too — the Hybrid Shield Magnet Case costs an eye-watering $100.

2. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra Case (Official)

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is the real continuation of the Z Fold 7 design, which could mean better luck with third-party cases. Still, it’s a good idea to go with Samsung’s first-party case if you want the best fit right out of the gate, and of those options, the Hybrid Shield Magnet case again seems like the best option for the most protection.

The main trouble with these cases is the price: it’s $100. Still, that can be worth it for a little peace of mind on day one.

Spigen is one of the longest-running phone case makers, and every case I’ve had from it has been solid. I’d expect no different from this case. It features a generous lip around the outside screen, a smooth, flat-backed design, and a hinge protector with built-in magnets to keep it covering your hinge. That last bit probably won’t mean it never flops off the folding edge of the phone, but it’s almost certainly less likely to break than the spring mechanism found in other Spigen phone cases.

This case is the only one of those Spigen shared with IGN ahead of Samsung’s official reveal that supports ultra-fast wireless charging, meaning it should reach up to 20W charging, or just five watts short of the full 25W offered by proper Qi2 support. And at just $30, I’m not mad at its price point.

Spigen is also my pick for rugged cases for the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, thanks to its thick design and its spring-loaded mechanism that keeps the hinge covering the most vulnerable point of the phone. The case takes a dual-layer approach, with raised bezels for the outer screen. According to Spigen, you’ll get ultra-fast wireless charging with the Tough Armor Pro MagFit, which has a magnetic ring on the back for Qi2 charging.

I have my doubts about the longevity of the spring mechanism, but if I’m spending this much money on a phone, I’d like to make sure the hinge is always protected. One thing to keep in mind is that the buttons aren’t covered. That’s one of those divisive things that some will like and others won’t (I’ve always preferred covered buttons, but only when it’s done well, which is rare.) Like the Air Fit Pro above, this case is blessedly cheap at $35.

5. Samsung Clear Magnet Case, Transparent

The Samsung first-party Clear Magnet Case is the obvious choice if you want to be able to see the colorful back panel of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 while it’s in a case, mainly because there’s no doubt it’ll fit your phone. It’s also embedded with a magnetic ring, a necessity if you want to take full advantage of MagSafe-like Qi2 wireless chargers.

At $60, this case also has the benefit of being cheaper than the other Samsung cases I listed above. Unfortunately, it appears to be made of the same soft TPU that has made up most clear cases forever, which means chances are good that in just a few months, it’ll have gained a dingy, yellow hue. Alas.

Dbrand’s Z Fold 8 and 8 Ultra case options are as numerous as they are fun to look at. The company is offering both the expansive patterned cases and a few solid-color options. The Grip Case has a rubbery grip around the outside that should make it easier to keep it in your hand (hence the name), and it will cover the edge of the front display, the hinge, and the back of the Z Fold 8 and 8 Ultra. It’s also got an integrated magnetic ring.

The cases cost up to $60, putting them on the pricey side compared to other third-party options. And Dbrand says they won’t ship until August, but not specifically when, so there’s the chance that it won’t arrive until after Galaxy Z Fold 8 and 8 Ultras start going out on August 7th.

I’ve never used a Benks case, but of the thin case options out there, I like this one for its hinge protection, which is not always a given in this category. Benks uses kevlar for its back case, a pliable TPU frame for the outer screen’s edge, and includes a glass screen protector for the front display. The case also has a magnetic ring embedded in the back edge for Qi2 wireless charging.

One potential issue I see here is that, based on one early video review I spotted online, the hinge protection doesn’t close automatically with the case, so you’ll need to remember to shut it yourself. Also, at $110, it ain’t even close to cheap. If hinge coverage isn’t really a concern, the next best thing could be the Thinborne Ultra Thin Aramid Fiber case, which costs “only” $90, or Samsung’s own $105 Carbon Magnet case.

The Benks ArmorGrid Pro for the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is, at $120, just a bit too rich for my blood. Despite its superior-seeming hinge coverage, I’d recommend the Thinborne Aramid Fiber option, instead. It costs just $90.

The major drawback is that it won’t totally cover the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra’s hinge, but that might not be an issue for this particular phone. After all, Samsung has been making practically the exact same design for many years – plenty of time to make it hold up to punishment.

paragraphs: Another year, another Galaxy Z Fold phone . The eighth iteration, if you can believe it. And actually, it’s not just one, but two phones this time: the same-as-it-ever-was Z Fold 8 Ultra that looks just like the Z Fold 7 , and the wider, passport-style Z Fold 8.

Before you pick a case for one of these phones, decide how much you want to compromise the look and feel of your phone, versus how much you want to protect it. As someone who sits at a desk all day, I like a slim case if I’m using one at all, despite what the chunky ESR clear case currently on my iPhone 15 Pro says. In my service industry days, I preferred something more protective, especially for something as damage-prone as a foldable.
Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Hybrid Shield Magnet Case
Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra Case (Official)

Phone makers don’t usually know for certain the precise dimensions and materials of a phone before it’s released, so my general recommendation is go with first-party cases, if you can afford it. Also, since these are brand new phones, keep in mind that this guide – like any others you encounter right as a phone has been released – is based on past experience with phone cases. For me, that’s about 17 years of slapping plastic, rubber and leather on my phones.
Check out the best Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra cases.
How to Pick a Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Case

Your first consideration when picking a case for your phone is to figure out what you want out of it. Are you looking for something slender to protect the phone from scratches? Something purely aesthetic to express yourself? Is it full-blown protection, in-hand comfort be damned?

Next, pick your ideal price range and line up your options. Look first for long-established brands, and if none of those have what you’re looking for, feel free to expand to those that haven’t been around as long. It’s hard to find case reviews these days, but cases have also just generally gotten better over the years, in my experience. Still, foldables remain a relatively young category, so it’s a good idea to find a reviewer whose tendencies jive with your own. I look for commentary about fit and hand-feel: does it want to pop off easily? Is it too hard to remove? Will it slip out of my hand? That sort of thing.

Finally, don’t forget that these are brand new phones and that case makers don’t all get advance information that lets them make a precise fit. Some brands are good about that, and will ship you a replacement as soon as they’re dialed in later. If you’re committed to a third-party option, make sure they at least offer that. Otherwise, if you know you’re clumsy or you just want a guarantee, go with a phone case that’s made, or at least approved, by Samsung itself.
1. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Hybrid Shield Magnet Case

Samsung’s official Galaxy Z Fold 8 case is usually your best bet right out of the gate, and that’ll be especially true in a year when the company has totally overhauled the physical dimensions of its mainstay foldable. Sure, there have been plenty of leaks that have let case makers generate products based on the actual dimensions of the phone, but without the real thing, they can’t truly test them.

The Hybrid Shield Magnet Case features a split-hinge-cover only thing is that first-party cases are pretty much always pricier than third-party options, and that’s true here, too — the Hybrid Shield Magnet Case costs an eye-watering $100.
2. Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra Case (Official)

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is the real continuation of the Z Fold 7 design, which could mean better luck with third-party cases. The main trouble with these cases is the price: it’s $100. Still, that can be worth it for a little peace of mind on day one.

Spigen is one of the longest-running phone case makers, and every case I’ve had from it has been solid. I’d expect no different from this case. articles.title: Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8 feels like the future
articles.summary: The Z Fold 8 looks unusual at first, with its squat outer screen, but you get used to it fast — and the wide inner display makes it all worthwhile.
articles.body: Is this the future of foldable phones?  Samsung clearly thinks so. The company has given its new wide foldable the “Z Fold 8” name, positioning the phone not as a widescreen oddity, but as the new normal, the default design for foldables going forward. Rumor has it that Apple feels the same way, with a similar squat shape widely predicted for the first foldable iPhone, expected to launch in September. Whether you want to give the credit to Apple, Samsung, or even Huawei (which got here first with the Pura X Max), I think they might be onto something. After a week, the Z Fold 8 feels comfortable, natural, and normal, despite being the shortest and widest phone I can remember using. And thanks to the 4:3 inner display — better suited to both reading and watching video — I’m using this as a foldable more than I ever have with previous models.  It isn’t perfect. Not every app plays nicely with the short outer screen, though issues are pretty rare. And the drop from three cameras on last year’s model to two cameras on this year’s feels like a real downgrade for an $1,899 phone. We won’t really know the future of foldables until Apple enters the market. But with the Z Fold 8, Samsung has already made a good case that this design should stick around.  [Product: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 | https://www.amazon.com/Samsung-Galaxy-Fold8-Unlocked-Phone/dp/B0H12P5KS7/?tag=theverge02-20, https://go.skimresources.com/?id=1025X1701640&xs=1&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.samsung.com%2Fus%2Fsmartphones%2Fgalaxy-z-fold8%2Fbuy%2Fgalaxy-z-fold8-256gb-unlocked-sku-sm-f971ulvaxaa%2F, https://bestbuy.7tiv.net/c/482924/614286/10014?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.bestbuy.com%2Fproduct%2Fsamsung-galaxy-z-fold8-256gb-unlocked-graphite%2FJJGRF3FS98] Until now, foldables have mostly been one of three shapes: flippy, foldy, and more recently (and rarely) trifoldy. Samsung has played a large part in defining those categories. But the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is among the first of a new wave of wider models. The 5.5-inch outer display is both shorter and wider than typical phones, almost the exact same dimensions as a standard passport, with a 10:16 aspect ratio. It looks a little odd when closed, but makes sense when you open the phone up to see its 7.6-inch, 4:3 inner screen — not coincidentally the exact aspect ratio used by most iPads. This feels more like a foldable tablet than any previous Z Fold yet, and perhaps because of that I’ve found myself opening it up more than any foldable I’ve ever reviewed. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268671_Samsung_Galaxy_Z_Fold_8_DPreston_0046.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268671_Samsung_Galaxy_Z_Fold_8_DPreston_0063.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268671_Samsung_Galaxy_Z_Fold_8_DPreston_0091.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268671_Samsung_Galaxy_Z_Fold_8_DPreston_0107.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] This stretched shape is more natural for watching TV and movies, giving you a wider screen without too much letterboxing. It’s much better suited to this than the Z Fold 8 Ultra, which barely gives you any extra screen space for video when held vertically and has its selfie camera cutout in the way if you rotate it into landscape. The Z Fold 8 is arguably even better for reading, giving a convincing facsimile of the dimensions of a book when you hold it in portrait. The shape takes more getting used to when closed, but less than you might think. Even when I tried the phone for an hour or so at Samsung’s press briefing I was surprised by how natural it felt, and a week with the Z Fold 8 has only cemented that feeling. After a while this doesn’t feel like an especially short or wide device, it just feels like a phone. There are occasional errors that give away that Android wasn’t designed with these dimensions in mind. Once or twice Instagram has failed to fully load, leaving a white bar in the extra space on the right-hand side of the screen; the Withings app once crunched two rows of content together in an effort to fit things in vertically; and even Samsung’s default One UI Quick Settings panel is too long, requiring you to scroll to reach the bottom. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268671_Samsung_Galaxy_Z_Fold_8_DPreston_0129.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268671_Samsung_Galaxy_Z_Fold_8_DPreston_0131.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] I’m not saying this squat screen is better than a regular slab phone, because it probably isn’t. You have to scroll a little more often because of the lost vertical space, and it can be a stretch to reach the phone’s far side. But there are advantages too: the extra width makes two-handed typing more comfortable (it’s not been much remarked, but this is a pretty similar size and shape to the classic BlackBerry); and because it’s so short, reaching the top of the phone is easier than ever. Anyone lamenting the death of the small phone may, perhaps paradoxically, find they’re a fan of the Z Fold 8. It helps that all that reduced size keeps the Z Fold 8 light. At 201g, it’s Samsung’s lightest Z Fold yet. It’s slim too. At 9.7mm thick when shut, this is just a little chunkier than last year’s Z Fold 7, or this year’s Ultra, but it’s still far thinner than 2024’s Z Fold 6. Those dimensions put it within reach of a standard smartphone; an iPhone 17 Pro, for instance, is 206g and 8.8mm thick. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268671_Samsung_Galaxy_Z_Fold_8_DPreston_0051.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268671_Samsung_Galaxy_Z_Fold_8_DPreston_0056.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Despite its slimness, the Z Fold 8 actually packs a bigger battery than any Z Fold bar the new Ultra, with a capacity of 4,800mAh. That’s thanks to Samsung finally adopting silicon-carbon batteries, a more energy-dense design that just about every Chinese phone manufacturer has long since adopted.  Samsung has been duly cautious in its approach, emphasizing stability and longevity as it’s incorporated more reactive silicon into the battery anode. Silicon-carbon batteries have a tendency to degrade faster than traditional designs, meaning the battery life gets worse more quickly over time, but Samsung says it’s managed to avoid that risk. It’ll take a year or more to learn just how well Samsung struck that balance, but for now I’m heading to bed with 40 percent of the battery left every night, so the extra capacity is doing its job. Charging is fine, but less impressive. The Z Fold 8 has 45W wired charging and 20W wireless, both of which are good by US standards but sluggish compared to many Android phones available elsewhere. Unlike Google’s Pixel 10 Pro Fold, the Z Fold 8 lacks the built-in magnets required to support Qi2 wireless charging, though it is compatible with Qi2 cases. In fairness, that helps keep the phone itself thinner and lighter, and Samsung is likely betting that you were going to put a case on it anyway. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268671_Samsung_Galaxy_Z_Fold_8_DPreston_0117.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268671_Samsung_Galaxy_Z_Fold_8_DPreston_0062.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268671_Samsung_Galaxy_Z_Fold_8_DPreston_0019.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268671_Samsung_Galaxy_Z_Fold_8_DPreston_0038.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] That’s a shame, because the phone looks great. It fits right into Samsung’s existing design language, which I’ve long been a fan of for its slick simplicity. I love my lavender model, in a simple, subtle purple, as well as the online-exclusive “pistachio” — though it’s really more of a grayish green than anything resembling the nut. There’s no IP68 rating, which is a shame, with IP48 protection leaving the Z Fold 8 a little more vulnerable to dust and sand than rival foldables from Google, Oppo, and Honor. Samsung says the phone is sturdier overall thanks to new titanium infused layers under the display, which also make the crease on the inner screen subtler. It’s not quite as difficult to see or feel as on Oppo’s impressive Find N6, but the crease really is a complete non-issue now. The cameras might be more of a concern. Samsung has downgraded the Z Fold 8 to just two rear lenses, a main camera and an ultrawide — no telephoto at all. And while the new 50-megapixel ultrawide is a significant improvement on what came before, the main camera uses a smaller sensor, lower resolution, and narrower aperture than the previous generation, making it worse in just about every respect. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260724_083615.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260723_210317-1.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260727_114727-1.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260724_204148.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260723_132306.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260725_173031.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260725_173033.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260723_210335.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260723_210341-1.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260723_203700.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260723_203656.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260724_004350.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260724_004347.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260728_193756.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The photos it takes are fine. This is a similar main camera to the base Galaxy S26, with similar results, and roughly comparable to an iPhone 17. The low-light processing is better than I expected so long as subjects are mostly still, and colors are vivid but attractive. Like many Samsung cameras it finds fast-moving subjects tricky — almost every photo I’ve attempted of either of my cats has been blurry. The setup is improved by the ultrawide, which matches the main lens on quality in almost every shot, meaning there’s rarely a tradeoff for zooming out. But at this price, a telephoto lens wouldn’t go amiss. Compared to previous generations of Z Fold, Samsung has kept the software updates fairly light. Google’s Gemini Intelligence Task Automation has rolled out to the phone, but isn’t yet available in the UK so I haven’t been able to test it. Then there’s My FanCam, an AI video editing feature which crops in to focus on a specific person. Now Nudge, Samsung’s take on Pixel phones’ Magic Cue, will suggest contextual actions you can carry out in split-screen, like adding an event to your calendar — though since it requires you to use Samsung Keyboard and specific messaging apps, it’s a little limited in practice. [Image: I never expected to like this phone so much. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268671_Samsung_Galaxy_Z_Fold_8_DPreston_0002.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The foldable market is going to change for good in a month or two’s time. Apple’s entry into the space could be the push foldables need to go mainstream, or the final proof that they’ll be forever niche.  Either way, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 makes a good case that this might be the shape their future hopes rest in. It’s compact enough to feel small when folded and wide enough to feel expansive when open. It’s great for watching TV and movies, but just as good for reading, the two things most people might actually want a foldable for, leaving the Ultra for the multitasking productivity obsessives. If I was buying one of Samsung’s new foldables, it would be this one. But while this feels like the future of foldables, it still needs to get substantially cheaper to become the future of phones. Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge --- Agree to Continue: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate. To use the Galaxy Z Fold 8, you must agree to: * Google Terms of Service * Google Play Terms of Service * Google Privacy Policy (included in ToS) * Install apps and updates: “You agree this device may also automatically download and install updates and apps from Google, your carrier, and your device’s manufacturer, possibly using cellular data.” * Samsung End User Licence Agreement * Samsung Privacy Notice * Samsung Terms and Conditions There’s also a variety of optional agreements, including: * Provide anonymous location data for Google’s services * “Allow apps and services to scan for Wi-Fi networks and nearby devices at any time, even when Wi-Fi or Bluetooth is off.” * Send usage and diagnostic data to Google * Google Gemini Apps Privacy Notice if you opt in to using Gemini Assistant * Turn on Samsung offline finding * Samsung news and special offers * Samsung personalized advertising * Bixby personal data intelligence * Samsung customization service Other features, like Google Wallet, may require additional agreements. Final tally: seven mandatory agreements and more than nine optional agreements. ---

There are occasional errors that give away that Android wasn’t designed with these dimensions in mind. Once or twice Instagram has failed to fully load, leaving a white bar in the extra space on the right-hand side of the screen; the Withings app once crunched two rows of content together in an effort to fit things in vertically; and even Samsung’s default One UI Quick Settings panel is too long, requiring you to scroll to reach the bottom. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268671_Samsung_Galaxy_Z_Fold_8_DPreston_0129.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268671_Samsung_Galaxy_Z_Fold_8_DPreston_0131.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] I’m not saying this squat screen is better than a regular slab phone, because it probably isn’t. You have to scroll a little more often because of the lost vertical space, and it can be a stretch to reach the phone’s far side. But there are advantages too: the extra width makes two-handed typing more comfortable (it’s not been much remarked, but this is a pretty similar size and shape to the classic BlackBerry); and because it’s so short, reaching the top of the phone is easier than ever. Anyone lamenting the death of the small phone may, perhaps paradoxically, find they’re a fan of the Z Fold 8. It helps that all that reduced size keeps the Z Fold 8 light. At 201g, it’s Samsung’s lightest Z Fold yet. It’s slim too. At 9.7mm thick when shut, this is just a little chunkier than last year’s Z Fold 7, or this year’s Ultra, but it’s still far thinner than 2024’s Z Fold 6. Those dimensions put it within reach of a standard smartphone; an iPhone 17 Pro, for instance, is 206g and 8.8mm thick. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268671_Samsung_Galaxy_Z_Fold_8_DPreston_0051.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268671_Samsung_Galaxy_Z_Fold_8_DPreston_0056.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Despite its slimness, the Z Fold 8 actually packs a bigger battery than any Z Fold bar the new Ultra, with a capacity of 4,800mAh. That’s thanks to Samsung finally adopting silicon-carbon batteries, a more energy-dense design that just about every Chinese phone manufacturer has long since adopted.  Samsung has been duly cautious in its approach, emphasizing stability and longevity as it’s incorporated more reactive silicon into the battery anode. Silicon-carbon batteries have a tendency to degrade faster than traditional designs, meaning the battery life gets worse more quickly over time, but Samsung says it’s managed to avoid that risk. It’ll take a year or more to learn just how well Samsung struck that balance, but for now I’m heading to bed with 40 percent of the battery left every night, so the extra capacity is doing its job. Charging is fine, but less impressive. The Z Fold 8 has 45W wired charging and 20W wireless, both of which are good by US standards but sluggish compared to many Android phones available elsewhere. Unlike Google’s Pixel 10 Pro Fold, the Z Fold 8 lacks the built-in magnets required to support Qi2 wireless charging, though it is compatible with Qi2 cases. In fairness, that helps keep the phone itself thinner and lighter, and Samsung is likely betting that you were going to put a case on it anyway. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268671_Samsung_Galaxy_Z_Fold_8_DPreston_0117.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268671_Samsung_Galaxy_Z_Fold_8_DPreston_0062.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268671_Samsung_Galaxy_Z_Fold_8_DPreston_0019.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268671_Samsung_Galaxy_Z_Fold_8_DPreston_0038.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] That’s a shame, because the phone looks great. It fits right into Samsung’s existing design language, which I’ve long been a fan of for its slick simplicity. I love my lavender model, in a simple, subtle purple, as well as the online-exclusive “pistachio” — though it’s really more of a grayish green than anything resembling the nut. There’s no IP68 rating, which is a shame, with IP48 protection leaving the Z Fold 8 a little more vulnerable to dust and sand than rival foldables from Google, Oppo, and Honor. Samsung says the phone is sturdier overall thanks to new titanium infused layers under the display, which also make the crease on the inner screen subtler. It’s not quite as difficult to see or feel as on Oppo’s impressive Find N6, but the crease really is a complete non-issue now. The cameras might be more of a concern. Samsung has downgraded the Z Fold 8 to just two rear lenses, a main camera and an ultrawide — no telephoto at all. And while the new 50-megapixel ultrawide is a significant improvement on what came before, the main camera uses a smaller sensor, lower resolution, and narrower aperture than the previous generation, making it worse in just about every respect. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260724_083615.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260723_210317-1.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260727_114727-1.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260724_204148.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260723_132306.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260725_173031.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260725_173033.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260723_210335.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260723_210341-1.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260723_203700.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260723_203656.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260724_004350.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260724_004347.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/20260728_193756.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The photos it takes are fine. This is a similar main camera to the base Galaxy S26, with similar results, and roughly comparable to an iPhone 17. The low-light processing is better than I expected so long as subjects are mostly still, and colors are vivid but attractive. Like many Samsung cameras it finds fast-moving subjects tricky — almost every photo I’ve attempted of either of my cats has been blurry. The setup is improved by the ultrawide, which matches the main lens on quality in almost every shot, meaning there’s rarely a tradeoff for zooming out. But at this price, a telephoto lens wouldn’t go amiss. Compared to previous generations of Z Fold, Samsung has kept the software updates fairly light. Google’s Gemini Intelligence Task Automation has rolled out to the phone, but isn’t yet available in the UK so I haven’t been able to test it. Then there’s My FanCam, an AI video editing feature which crops in to focus on a specific person. Now Nudge, Samsung’s take on Pixel phones’ Magic Cue, will suggest contextual actions you can carry out in split-screen, like adding an event to your calendar — though since it requires you to use Samsung Keyboard and specific messaging apps, it’s a little limited in practice. [Image: I never expected to like this phone so much. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268671_Samsung_Galaxy_Z_Fold_8_DPreston_0002.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The foldable market is going to change for good in a month or two’s time. Apple’s entry into the space could be the push foldables need to go mainstream, or the final proof that they’ll be forever niche.  Either way, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 makes a good case that this might be the shape their future hopes rest in. It’s compact enough to feel small when folded and wide enough to feel expansive when open. It’s great for watching TV and movies, but just as good for reading, the two things most people might actually want a foldable for, leaving the Ultra for the multitasking productivity obsessives. If I was buying one of Samsung’s new foldables, it would be this one. But while this feels like the future of foldables, it still needs to get substantially cheaper to become the future of phones. Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge --- Agree to Continue: Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate. To use the Galaxy Z Fold 8, you must agree to: * Google Terms of Service * Google Play Terms of Service * Google Privacy Policy (included in ToS) * Install apps and updates: “You agree this device may also automatically download and install updates and apps from Google, your carrier, and your device’s manufacturer, possibly using cellular data.” * Samsung End User Licence Agreement * Samsung Privacy Notice * Samsung Terms and Conditions There’s also a variety of optional agreements, including: * Provide anonymous location data for Google’s services * “Allow apps and services to scan for Wi-Fi networks and nearby devices at any time, even when Wi-Fi or Bluetooth is off.” * Send usage and diagnostic data to Google * Google Gemini Apps Privacy Notice if you opt in to using Gemini Assistant * Turn on Samsung offline finding * Samsung news and special offers * Samsung personalized advertising * Bixby personal data intelligence * Samsung customization service Other features, like Google Wallet, may require additional agreements. Final tally: seven mandatory agreements and more than nine optional agreements. ---

articles.title: Blacklyte Atlas Lite Standing Desk Review: Solid Features at Half the Price
articles.summary: The problem with a good standing desk is usually its price. Enter Blacklyte and its Atlas Lite Standing Desk. As the "Lite" in the name suggests, it has fewer frills than other standing desks, including the company's own Atlas, but at half the price, you're giving up surprisingly little from a practical standpoint.
articles.body:
We all know by now that even if you have a great chair , sitting for too long brings a myriad of musculoskeletal and metabolic risks. That's why standing desks , which can move to almost anywhere within their range to accommodate the most ergonomic positioning, are such game changers. The problem with a good standing desk, however, is usually its price. Enter Blacklyte and its Atlas Lite Standing Desk . As the "Lite" in the name suggests, it has fewer frills than other standing desks, including the company's own Atlas , but at half the price, you're giving up surprisingly little from a practical standpoint.

Blacklyte Atlas Lite – Options, Assembly, and Setup

The Atlas Lite Standing Desk is available in Obsidian Black, Moonstone White, and Natural Oak colorways. The Obsidian Black is the same color throughout, while the Moonstone White retains the black control panel. The Natural Oak is identical to the Moonstone White, except it features a Natural Oak-colored desktop.

The Obsidian Black is available in Small (47.2 inch width), Medium (55.1 inch width), and Large (63 inch width) sizes. The Moonstone White and Natural Oak are available in Medium, Large, and Extra Large (70.9 inch width) sizes. Small and Medium desktops can handle up to 220 lbs of distributed weight, while Large and Extra Large can handle up to 265 lbs.

All four desktop sizes feature a depth of 31.5 inches, which is on the generous side in comparison to other desks, standing or otherwise. This extra room can easily accommodate large or multiple monitors, allowing you to stand or sit back at a more comfortable distance.

I received the Obsidian Black in Medium, which came in two boxes. The desktop box weighed a beefy 73.6 lbs, with the desktop itself coming in at around 60.2 lbs. The box with the two legs came in at 50 lbs, with the legs themselves roughly 46.3 lbs, thanks to each one having its own motor.

It's not a difficult build, but it definitely requires two people because of all that weight. For the step that involved attaching the feet to the legs, I found that having a third person helped with alignment. In any case, you mostly use the included Allen key to secure the screws, building the legs first, then attaching them to the desktop.

There's a wire cover for the center underside crossbar, which is used to run the cables from the legs to the control panel. The control panel, which can be placed on the far right or far left of the desktop, is attached with different screws using the included Phillips screwdriver. The same screwdriver is then used to attach a cable management box to the rear of the desktop. Finally, the AC adapter is plugged into the control panel and then into the wall.

Blacklyte Atlas Lite – Form and Functionality

The recycled woodfibre desktop material has a nice glossy melamine laminate finish and rounded corners. Save for the flashy Blacklyte logo on the lower left corner of the desktop, it's an elegant design. As expected for a glossy surface, however, it does pick up a lot of fingerprints, so be sure to have a good microfiber cloth on call.

A metal frame runs along the perimeter of the underside of the desktop. This is great for stability, but does create a 2.3 inch thick surface, which can limit what you attach. I found clamp-style accessories work best, but even then, you have to make sure they can open up enough to fit. There's also a centered indent at the back of the desktop that's great for routing cables behind, particularly in conjunction with the cable tray that's directly underneath.

The plastic control panel is a bit flimsy and basic, but it has all of the functionality you need. Besides the up and down buttons, there are four memory presets, which are set at the current position by holding the number down until it beeps. Thanks to the dual motors, you don't have to wait long for the desk to quietly rise or lower. It only takes about 16 seconds to go from its lowest possible height of 27.5 inches to its highest of 46 inches. While more expensive standing desks may go a bit faster and better accommodate individuals taller than 6 feet 2 inches, for most needs, this should be plenty. However, if you're 6 feet 4 inches or taller, definitely look for a standing desk that can go to 48 inches or higher for better ergonomics.

The desk is reasonably solid thanks to the weight and metal frame, although there's some shake when not at a lower, seated height. A stability crossbar between the two legs would have probably helped provide that last bit of extra shake resistance, but its omission does keep the under-desk area far more usable.

Speaking of stability, I have a love/hate relationship with monitor arms. I love the concept, but have rarely found a monitor arm that remains reasonably stable, yet versatile. Fortunately, the optional Atlas Monitor Arm ($149, but like the desk, often on sale) is more in the love category. It's well-built overall and extremely adjustable.

The Atlas Monitor Arm simply clamp mounts in the area behind the desk that has a slight indent. I had no issue attaching it to a 34 inch LG Ultrawide Monitor. One disappointment was that one of the plastic cable clips arrived broken, so that's one thing the company can definitely improve. Otherwise, it's a great first party accessory.

While the Atlas Lite Standing Desk lacks the lighting, magnetic surface, and some of the other features found in the standard Atlas, it's hard to say that most of those are really necessary. Blacklyte made pretty good calls in regards to the essentials when getting the price down to where it is.

articles.title: Tony Tells the Tale of Anthony Bourdain's Teenage Years as the Famed Chef Winds Up on a Journey of Culinary Discovery
articles.summary: Tony review: Matt Johnson zeroes in on a teenage chapter in Anthony Bourdain’s life.
articles.body:
Tony will be released in select theaters on August 7 before expanding nationwide on August 21.

Eschewing the birth-to-death structure of celebrity biopics — as well as estate-mandated aggrandizing — Matt Johnson’s Tony focuses on a few chapters in the life of Anthony Bourdain from his 2000 memoir, Kitchen Confidential: Adventures in the Culinary Underbelly. During a summer spent in Cape Cod in the mid-1970s, teenage Tony learns for the first time that food, travel, and culture might be his forté. However, the late chef is hardly painted with a hagiographic brush; in fact, actor Dominic Sessa ( The Holdovers ) builds on minor details from the book, like Bourdain’s cocky swagger and the ridiculous nunchucks he kept tucked into his belt, to create an insolent, selfish, but ultimately driven version of a man whose name we’d come to know.

The movie is a blast, ensuring that Johnson is two-for-two this year alongside his time travel mockumentary, Nirvanna the Band the Show the Movie ; however, the two films could not be more different in scope and style. If anything, Tony — a more measured and intentional work — shares its tonal DNA with Johnson’s BlackBerry , an intense tale of innovators and eventual failures, which grew out of the post- Social Network tech biopic boom. It also wouldn’t be a stretch to call Tony one of the only films to truly understand and recreate what made The Social Network tick: the energy of naïve youth, no matter how destructive.

Part dramatic biography, part coming-of-age comedy, and wholly exciting, Tony begins with a highly fictionalized chapter in Bourdain’s life that sees him fibbing about a writing fellowship at Vassar so he can follow his high school crush, Nancy (Emilia Jones), to Cape Cod. The self-proclaimed author has dreams of grandeur and waxes poetic to anyone who’ll listen (drunkenly, might I add), even if it gets him in hot water. The next thing he knows, he’s working as a dishwasher in a local clam joint to make ends meet while keeping this lowly job a secret from his college peers, and sleeping on the porch hammock of his unnamed Portuguese boss, known only as “Chef” (Antonio Banderas).

The plot follows the growing proximity between Tony and Nancy in the perpetual dusk of Provincetown, but it also sees the young teen learning about the adult world — not only through his boss’ passions and failures, but through the drug-fueled sexual exploits of his coworker, Sal (Leo Woodall). Every male role model in Tony’s life seems to harbor a mysterious melancholy, leading to a fascinating set of performances from the cast. Woodall hides an aggrieved sadness just behind his eyes, while Banderas appears to live with regrets he’s long come to terms with. However, these are mere clues that inform each casual interaction rather than eclipsing the central drama. Ultimately, the mile-a-minute bustle of the cramped kitchen is where the movie lives and breathes, from the uncouth rituals of other supporting players (one particularly verbose cook is played by comedian Stavros Halkias) to the slow transition of Bourdain’s own POV on his new lot in life.

The film adapts only two short initial chapters of Kitchen Confidential, so apart from the broad details of time and place, it may as well be fiction. However, Johnson imbues the story with the spirit of Bourdain himself, capturing not only the tone of his writing (snappy, yet colorful), but the gradual widening of his perspective to consider food as a passion, an art form, and a series of local traditions. Most importantly, it reconnects artistry and artist as broad concepts, refusing to divorce creativity from even the most selfish emotional impulses. If The Social Network reframed Facebook as a romantic wound made manifest in isolation, Tony treats Bourdain’s culinary explorations as stemming from romantic pursuit while surrounded by community.

If the movie drops the ball in one notable way, it’s that Nancy is never quite fleshed out beyond this function in the story, making for some awkward (and at times retrograde) “get the girl” framing. However, Tony also unfolds through the perspective of a hot-blooded teenage boy, and includes all the things a lanky ne’er-do-well like Sessa’s Bourdain might find fascinating or alluring. It moves at the speed of rose-tinted thought, with careful visual compositions that get the point across instantaneously so they can be edited together with controlled chaos. All the while, Sessa makes for a fascinating centerpiece as a young man in search of himself, but with no way to find the right questions, let alone the answers, until he hurts those around him and learns from his mistakes.

It’s a feel-good guy movie in the vein of Richard Linklater’s Everybody Wants Some!! , another college period piece that similarly gazes backward in time while immersing you in its testosterone-drenched escapades, but with enough intellectual distance to excuse its visceral delights as a matter of nostalgic retrospective. It grants permission, in a way, to return to a time when the world seemed so large that anything could be possible, even when the weight of expectations bore down on you with unrelenting force.

It’s perhaps no coincidence that as much as Sessa channels the spirit of Bourdain, he also resembles Johnson himself in look and fast-talking demeanor. This ensures that Tony’s exploration of creative spark as something impure but no less valuable feels deeply personal too, as though the film were about eking out a daring space for filmmaking in the Canadian landscape in the way that Johnson and his cohorts often have. Either way, the result is a biopic laser-focused on the follies of youth and hyper-charged with all its vigor.

All the while, Sessa makes for a fascinating centerpiece as a young man in search of himself, but with no way to find the right questions, let alone the answers, until he hurts those around him and learns from his mistakes.

It’s a feel-good guy movie in the vein of Richard Linklater’s Everybody Wants Some!! , another college period piece that similarly gazes backward in time while immersing you in its testosterone-drenched escapades, but with enough intellectual distance to excuse its visceral delights as a matter of nostalgic retrospective. It grants permission, in a way, to return to a time when the world seemed so large that anything could be possible, even when the weight of expectations bore down on you with unrelenting force.

It’s perhaps no coincidence that as much as Sessa channels the spirit of Bourdain, he also resembles Johnson himself in look and fast-talking demeanor. This ensures that Tony’s exploration of creative spark as something impure but no less valuable feels deeply personal too, as though the film were about eking out a daring space for filmmaking in the Canadian landscape in the way that Johnson and his cohorts often have. Either way, the result is a biopic laser-focused on the follies of youth and hyper-charged with all its vigor.

articles.title: Best Buy is selling an RTX 5080 for more than the RTX 5090’s MSRP
articles.summary: Best Buy has increased the price of an RTX 5080 GPU to $2,099, higher than the MSRP of Nvidia’s RTX 5090 and double the RTX 5080’s MSRP.
articles.body: Best Buy has raised the price of the Asus ROG Astral RTX 5080 OC to $2,099 — the first time a major US retailer is directly selling an RTX 5080 for more than the $1,999 MSRP of the RTX 5090, VideoCardz reports. The ROG Astral RTX 5080 OC now costs 40 percent more than its launch price of $1,499, and over double the $999 MSRP of the RTX 5080 Founders Edition.  As VideoCardz notes, this is currently the only RTX 5080 directly sold by Best Buy that’s priced over the RTX 5090’s MSRP. There are still other RTX 5080 GPUs available for significantly less, including at other retailers — Asus is selling the ROG Astral RTX 5080 OC for $1,899, which is still more than its launch price but a bit lower than Best Buy. However, component shortages and RAM price hikes aren’t showing any sign of slowing down any time soon, so more RTX 5080 GPUs could see similar price hikes.  Best Buy’s price increase also follows reports that Nvidia is planning to increase its GPU prices by 20 to 30 percent, its third such price hike this year. With prices for RAM and other components rising, we’ve even seen the return of GPUs with 4GB of VRAM like the ASRock AMD Radeon RX 9050 Challenger.
