articles.title: HP’s HyperX Omen 15 isn’t quite the budget-friendly gaming laptop its predecessor was
articles.summary: The HyperX Omen 15 gaming laptop offers an Intel Raptor Lake chip and Nvidia RTX 5050 graphics. But while its predecessor cost $800, the Omen is now a $1,200 affair.
articles.body: The HP HyperX Omen 15, which I first saw at CES, replaces the HP Victus 15, a longtime bestselling budget gaming laptop. The Victus cost just $800, or less when on sale, and was a good entry point to decent laptop gaming. The Omen 15 has nice little upgrades over the Victus. Its RTX 5050 Laptop GPU can play 2026’s latest games, albeit on low-ish settings. But it’s also got a brighter 16:10 aspect ratio display with higher refresh rate, and a 1080p webcam to make it a little better for non-gaming stuff.  I’d call it a working-class gaming laptop, but thanks to RAMageddon, the Omen 15 starts at $1,200 — a far cry from the $800 that made its predecessor so appealing. But laptop prices are way up across the board, and if you want current-gen gaming hardware, this is about as cheap as you’re going to find it. [Product: HyperX Omen 15 (Intel Core 5 210H, RTX 5050) | https://goto.walmart.com/c/482924/565706/9383?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.walmart.com%2Fip%2FHP-OMEN-Gaming-Notebook-15-3-2K-Intel-Core-5-16-RAM-512-SSD-Nvidia-RTX-5050-Black%2F18153321068] --- Component report card * Screen: C * Webcam: C * Keyboard: C * Trackpad: D * Port selection: C * Speakers: C * Number of ugly stickers to remove: 3 --- Our HyperX Omen 15 review unit is a $1,199 configuration sold through Walmart with an eight-core Intel Core 5 210H “Raptor Lake” chip, RTX 5050 discreet GPU, 16GB of DDR5 RAM, and 512GB SSD. There are pricier Omen 15 configs out there with RTX 5070 GPUs and OLED screens, but that’s like spending Acura money on a Honda Civic. On the lower end, HP still has a Victus 15 config with the RTX 5050 for $900, but it has 8GB of RAM — that’s not really tenable, especially for playing the latest games. The good news is that the Omen 15 with an RTX 5050 is pretty serviceable for playing games at its 1920 x 1200 native resolution. Last-gen games like Control can get a smooth 70 to 80fps on High preset while using DLSS. Cyberpunk 2077 can run on the Ultra preset (no ray tracing) with DLSS set to Quality and get 60 to 70fps— sometimes dipping down to 40 while driving with lots of stuff onscreen. Standard frame generation boosts it to 95 to 105fps, and 70s to low 80s in a car. Multi Frame Gen, which you don’t get on last-gen GPUs, can push that ever further if you don’t mind more “fake frames.”  Newer games are a more Medium to Low affair. For example, Helldivers 2 runs comfortably at just above 60fps on its Medium preset with DLSS set to Quality — though it dips into the 40s when the bug guts hit the fan. But Battlefield 6 was lower, down in the 50fps range while running Medium preset with DLSS cranked to Performance. I also tested Halo: Campaign Evolved, which defaulted to its Very Low preset, where it looked like a potato. On Low settings, with DLSS set to Medium, it mustered between 50 to 60fps, but with frequent drops into the 40s with lots of enemies onscreen.  [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268675_HP_HyperX_Omen_15_gaming_laptop_ADiBenedetto_0007.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268675_HP_HyperX_Omen_15_gaming_laptop_ADiBenedetto_0006.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268675_HP_HyperX_Omen_15_gaming_laptop_ADiBenedetto_0009.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] While playing all these games, the fans kicked up to a decent volume, but they weren’t obnoxiously loud, and the chassis stayed reasonably cool. The hottest point, a small spot under the chassis, rose to 113 degrees Fahrenheit / 45 Celsius. But the main areas that normally make contact with your hands or lap didn’t get too warm — pretty good thermals for a somewhat compact gaming laptop. So the RTX 5050 GPU and its 8GB of VRAM can get by with the latest graphically intense games, so long as you’re not expecting a visual powerhouse. But what about living with the rest of the laptop?  Much of the Omen 15’s price has gone to its specs. That means there are some rough edges showing in the usual areas. The trackpad has a responsive mechanical click, but if you pick up the laptop by either of its front corners the chassis flexes and causes an accidental click. This is common in mostly plastic laptops, but still annoying. The keyboard has decent enough tactility when typing. But even though I know gamers love a number pad, it makes this 15-inch laptop feel cramped. I don’t enjoy typing on it like I have other HP laptops. The speakers? A little muddy-sounding — especially for music. And the ports? It has HDMI 2.1 and gigabit ethernet, which is great, but only one USB-C to go with its two USB-A ports. And all of them are a modest 10Gbps — not particularly speedy compared to USB4 or Thunderbolt 4. Gaming laptops are supposed to have ports aplenty, but this is just ports apassable. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268675_HP_HyperX_Omen_15_gaming_laptop_ADiBenedetto_0004.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268675_HP_HyperX_Omen_15_gaming_laptop_ADiBenedetto_0002.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268675_HP_HyperX_Omen_15_gaming_laptop_ADiBenedetto_0015.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268675_HP_HyperX_Omen_15_gaming_laptop_ADiBenedetto_0016.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268675_HP_HyperX_Omen_15_gaming_laptop_ADiBenedetto_0010.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268675_HP_HyperX_Omen_15_gaming_laptop_ADiBenedetto_0008.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268675_HP_HyperX_Omen_15_gaming_laptop_ADiBenedetto_0013.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Aside from its gaming performance, the Omen 15’s other strength is its screen. The 1920 x 1200 IPS panel isn’t particularly special, but at 400 nits it’s decently bright and it has nice contrast and colors. It’s good for games, and fine for productivity work and light content creation. I did a bit of Lightroom Classic editing on the Omen 15, and my 50-megapixel RAW files were workable at a modest clip. (It helped that I was editing a batch of under 50 images, and not, like, 2,000.) The bigger problem with trying to do creative things was the Omen’s paltry 512GB of storage. It fills up quickly when games like Battlefield 6 take up 142GB. There’s a second M.2 slot for another drive, just as there’s a second RAM slot, which is great for future upgrades — but boy will that cost you right now. You can hold out for RAM and SSD prices to come back down to Earth, but if that takes as long as it’s expected to, the Omen 15 might feel pretty outdated by then. The Omen was also fine for my everyday work: Chrome tabs, four virtual desktops, Signal, Slack, music streaming, etc. While the 1080p webcam is a little grainy and slightly low in saturation, it looks fine on video calls. The main barrier to getting work done on the Omen 15 is that its battery never lasted me more than five and a half hours. That’s far from the worst for gaming laptops, but keep that chunky power adapter with its barrel plug nearby. [Image: That HyperX lid logo still doesn’t look great to me, but I’m getting used to ignoring it. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268675_HP_HyperX_Omen_15_gaming_laptop_ADiBenedetto_0011.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The HyperX Omen 15 is a decent gaming laptop. It’s just not the value the Victus 15 used to be. But neither is anything else. Absent a really good sale, you’re going to pay over $1,000 for anything with the RTX 5050, and usually a lot more. But buying into even the bottom rung of the 50-series gets you all of Nvidia’s latest features, like Multi Frame Gen and whatever DLSS 5 eventually shapes up to be. Last-gen 40-series or AMD GPUs aren’t bad options, but Multi Frame Gen can help keep frame rates playable for longer. It’s still worth looking for those sales, though. HP, Best Buy, and Walmart often have deals on most of HP’s product line. Even now, there’s an Omen 16 with an RTX 5060 GPU and slightly larger (but dimmer) screen for just $100 more than the Omen 15.  RAMageddon makes buying a new gaming laptop daunting. If you need to buy now and you don’t want to go open-box or secondhand, you just have to come to terms with the fact that you’re going to be paying higher prices than equivalent models from a year or two ago — even in the “entry level.” Considering the circumstances, the Omen 15 is an okay value at $1,200 for getting into laptop gaming. --- HyperX Omen 15 specs (as reviewed) * Display: 15.3-inch 1920 x 1200 165Hz IPS, 400 nits, anti-glare * CPU: Intel Core 5 210H (Raptor Lake, 8 cores) * GPU: Nvidia GeForce RTX 5050 * RAM: 16GB DDR5 (two SODIMM slots, user-accessible) * Storage: 512GB NVMe M.2 (two slots, user-accessible) * Webcam: 1080p * Connectivity: Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 5.3 * Ports: 2x USB-A 10Gbps, 1x USB-C 10Gbps, AC power (barrel plug), HDMI 2.1, RJ-45 gigabit ethernet, 3.5mm combo audio jack * Biometrics: none (lockscreen password only) * Weight: 5 pounds / 2.27kg * Dimensions: 13.5 x 9.96 x 0.89 - 0.93 inches / 342.9 x 252.98 x 22.61 - 23.62mm * Battery: 70Wh * Price: $1,199 --- Photography by Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge [Table: Benchmark comparisons]

articles.title: The Targaryens Remind Us Why Their Civil War Is Called the Dance of Dragons in This Week's Lizard-Rich Episode of House of the Dragon
articles.summary: House of the Dragon Season 3, Episode 7 Recap and Review: The Targaryens remind us why their civil war is called the Dance of Dragons in a lizard-rich episode.
articles.body:
Full spoilers follow for House of the Dragon Season 3, Episode 7.

There’s a great fundamental issue at the heart of House Targaryen that has too often gone unexamined and underexplained in House of the Dragon, despite its name, and that’s how the dragons work. This show has followed its predecessor’s example in leaning into the human drama of Westeros and away from its more fantastical aspects, but there’s a limit to how well that works, and in this engaging and generally fun episode (unless you’re Emma D’Arcy’s Rhaenyra), they finally get their teeth, and claws, into it.

The question is what, exactly, is the relationship between rider and dragon for House Targaryen and their allies? What are the obligations between rider and beast, if any? How (or how much) do they communicate? Do their feelings affect one another? There have been suggestions, occasionally, that having a dragon may affect one’s temperament (or that one’s temperament may affect one’s chance of bonding with a dragon); there’s a clear implication that losing your dragon is a form of emasculation for Tom Glynn-Carney’s Aegon II and the late Viserys (Paddy Considine). But it’s never been clear if it matters, and how much, beyond prestige in the internal Targaryen pecking order.

This time, however, we get some key hints that there’s more of a link than perhaps we were shown before. The scenes of dragon conflict, as when Rhaenyra finally discovers that her husband Daemon (Matt Smith) has been lying to her to protect his daughter Rhaena (Phoebe Campbell) and flies to confront both along with Addam (Clinton Liberty), suggest an emotional closeness. As the humans shout at one another, their dragons roar and bellow and, occasionally, threaten to flame, and it’s absolutely clear that they’re reflecting something human and vice versa. Later in the episode we see Aegon screaming in sync with his steed Sunfyre, both disfigured and defiant and apparently on the verge of madness, and the impression is confirmed.

The episode also begins with a dream of Helaena (Phia Saban) and in fact heavily features her dreams - or perhaps Dreams, of the prophetic kind. So what does it mean that she sees herself on her dragon, Dreamfyre, shouting “Dracarys!” as an angry mob rushes at them in the Dragonpit? What does it mean that she imagines a quiet life on the farm with her children (it looks like both Jaehaera and a younger boy, presumably the one she’s currently expecting) when an eclipse occurs? Rhaenyra is putting her younger half-sister under pressure to share her Dreams, desperate for reassurance that she is on the right path, but it’s not clear that Helaena has any such comfort to offer.

Of course, that’s far from the most screwed-up dream this episode. That prize goes to Aemond (Ewan Mitchell), who sees his mother Alicent (Olivia Cooke) arriving at Harrenhal and the two of them tumbling into bed together before realising it was all a dream. And then he wakes up and she has indeed arrived. Awkward! This may not be the dictionary definition of “headfuck” but it should be. Alicent babbles, Aemond is more taciturn, Alys (Gayle Rankin) is rightly suspicious of the newcomer. Aemond shares her wariness to a degree, enough to murder Alicent’s travelling companion (who, to be fair, is there to help assassinate him), but not enough to refuse the poisoned nightcap she offers after the world’s most awkward meet-the-mother-in-law dinner. Alicent creeps out of the castle and into the wind, figuring that the job is done and stricken by it, but Aemond stumbles to Alys at the first stomach pangs so he’ll probably recover.

Meanwhile Rhaenyra is still pulled in every direction and failing to deal with any of her problems, and it creates a vacuum at the seat of her power. Torrhen Manderly (Dan Fogler) is furious that he’s been left to hold the bag for everyone’s money woes – something that is literally his job -- and Mysaria (Sonoya Mizuno) is trying to make herself a conduit to the people and being rejected on all sides. She manages to, ahem, reconnect with Rhaenyra herself by the end of the episode (is that what the kids are calling it these days?), but she’s still caught in-between a regal rock and a common hard place, and that’s a tough situation to be in.

Daemon, too, is looking more woebegone than we have seen him before. He has belatedly realised that his daughter may desperately need him, which by Westeros standards makes him father of the year against almost zero competition, but in trying to protect her he has broken his wife’s heart. And also, he’s almost entirely failed to protect her; he’s just separated her from her dragon and gone home. He’s also increasingly floundering in council, suffering the same myopia as Rhaenyra and failing to look past his personal passions to the big picture.

It’s a mess. The only person laughing – and laughing a lot this time -- is Ormund (James Norton), who’s riding high despite the imminent arrival of the Rivermen outside his hastily built walls and the fact that he’s probably in last place in that aforementioned father of the year competition. He holds Corlys Velaryon (Steve Toussaint) captive, and cuts off his finger as proof of life to attempt to keep the Velaryon men from plugging the policing gap in King’s Landing (an efficient and speedy postal system still appears to be operating between Tumbleton and King’s Landing). He’s also keeping his ward Daeron (Benjamin Evan Ainsworth) and cousin Gwayne (Freddie Fox) in the dark about his plans, to their increasing frustration. And, in the episode’s final big reveal, he’s courting the dragon rider Ulf (Tom Bennett), trying to turn him from Rhaenyra’s service with the promise that he’ll become Lord of (Corlys’) Driftmark fortress, and also that he’ll be free to drink whenever he wants. It’s not clear which is the bigger inducement to the big ol’ lush but it could spell big trouble for Rhaenyra if he turns.

So the tally was six dragons for Rhaenyra (Syrax, Caraxes, Vermithor, Silverwing, Moondancer, Seasmoke) plus one unreliable wannabe ally (Sheepstealer). Then there was one MIA for the Greens (Vhagar) and one out of combat (Dreamfyre). Now there are five for Rhaenyra, two of them perhaps injured; two for the Greens (it looks like Ulf’s Silverwing and the resurgent Sunfyre) and potentially two MIA dragons (Sheepstealer and Vhagar, still) to potentially change that calculus further. It’s all at play going into the Season 3 finale, and it’s still not clear how far these flames could spread.
paragraphs: Full spoilers follow for House of the Dragon Season 3, Episode 7.

There’s a great fundamental issue at the heart of House Targaryen that has too often gone unexamined and underexplained in House of the Dragon, despite its name, and that’s how the dragons work. This show has followed its predecessor’s example in leaning into the human drama of Westeros and away from its more fantastical aspects, but there’s a limit to how well that works, and in this engaging and generally fun episode (unless you’re Emma D’Arcy’s Rhaenyra), they finally get their teeth, and claws, into it.

The question is what, exactly, is the relationship between rider and dragon for House Targaryen and their allies? What are the obligations between rider and beast, if any? How (or how much) do they communicate? Do their feelings affect one another? There have been suggestions, occasionally, that having a dragon may affect one’s temperament (or that one’s temperament may affect one’s chance of bonding with a dragon); there’s a clear implication that losing your dragon is a form of emasculation for Tom Glynn-Carney’s Aegon II and the late Viserys (Paddy Considine). But it’s never been clear if it matters, and how much, beyond prestige in the internal Targaryen pecking order.

This time, however, we get some key hints that there’s more of a link than perhaps we were shown before. The scenes of dragon conflict, as when Rhaenyra finally discovers that her husband Daemon (Matt Smith) has been lying to her to protect his daughter Rhaena (Phoebe Campbell) and flies to confront both along with Addam (Clinton Liberty), suggest an emotional closeness. As the humans shout at one another, their dragons roar and bellow and, occasionally, threaten to flame, and it’s absolutely clear that they’re reflecting something human and vice versa. Later in the episode we see Aegon screaming in sync with his steed Sunfyre, both disfigured and defiant and apparently on the verge of madness, and the impression is confirmed.

The episode also begins with a dream of Helaena (Phia Saban) and in fact heavily features her dreams - or perhaps Dreams, of the prophetic kind. So what does it mean that she sees herself on her dragon, Dreamfyre, shouting “Dracarys!” as an angry mob rushes at them in the Dragonpit? articles.title: Is the Ultra-Thin Motorola Razr Fold Worth Its $1,899 Price Tag? We Put Its Gaming Performance, Cameras, and Battery to the Test to Find Out.
articles.summary: Motorola packs it all in for this foldable, providing great screens, cameras, performance and features, even if it does end up a bit expensive.
articles.body:
The Motorola Razr Fold takes the Razr family to a new dimension. While earlier foldables from Motorola followed in the footsteps of the original Razr, offering a flip-phone style footprint, the Razr Fold opts for a hotdog fold, akin to what Samsung has offered from its Galaxy Z Fold lineup. Motorola hasn’t taken generations of iterations on this design to get to a very solid point, though. The Razr Fold is impressively thin and looks like all the experience gained from the earlier Razr foldables is paying off big. At $1,899, it’s not a cheap option, but it may still have what it takes to earn your money or at least due consideration.

Motorola Razr Fold – Design and Features

As mentioned, the Razr Fold opens like a book rather than an old school flip phone. Where Samsung’s early folders were normal-size while open and double the thickness of a typical smartphone while closed, the Razr Fold has jumped straight to ultra-thin dimensions.

Closed up, it looks almost like any other smartphone, and it’s a pretty one with a textured, rubberized back. It’s a little thicker than most, and the camera bump adds quite a bit of depth (that’ll prove worthwhile), but it doesn’t feel unusually large. Unfolded, it becomes impressively thin at 0.19 inches to edge out even the Samsung Galaxy S25 Edge or iPhone Air – camera bumps aside. The hints that it’s a foldable are the asymmetry and the seem running around the perimeter of the phone. It is a bit on the heavy side at 8.6 ounces, but that’s not so crazy next to the 8 ounce iPhone 16 Pro Max .

Folded shut, the 21:9 exterior display is a large 6.6-inch, 1080x2520 panel, and it opens up to reveal an even larger, nearly square 8.1-inch, 2232x2484 internal display. Both screens are sharp and bright LTPO pOLED displays with the internal reaching 120Hz and the external hitting 165Hz. For ultra-wide cinema, the external display will probably be the one to go with, and then it won’t really stand out from the crowd of bigger flagship phone displays. But for the wealth of 16:9 content out there (or even squarer formats like 4:3 or The Snyder Cut ), the internal display can provide a larger surface for viewing than the competition. That inner seam where the phone folds remains a minor nuisance. It shows glare readily, and it’s all the more apparent when displaying dark content or viewed at an off angle. You can also easily feel it when swiping across. That said, when the screen is lit up and you face it head-on, the seam mostly vanishes.

Either way, both screens can look gorgeous in the right conditions, and even though they love to show finger oils and glare on the interior folding seam is apparent, they push out enough brightness to easily get past that glare. You won’t want to treat the two displays the same, though. The exterior has Gorilla Glass Ceramic 3 that should withstand drops and scrapes a lot better than the internal display’s Ultra Thin Glass.

While you’ll want to be gentle with the phone, it’s still tougher than early foldables. It has an IP49 rating to keep a good deal of dust and debris out (just don’t fold it closed with a bunch of crud inside. It can also withstand submersion in freshwater and water jets.

It’s truly a shame we as a body of consumers let smartphone makers get away with killing the microSD card slot, because the Razr Fold likely could have had one. The SIM try in the phone is extra long, with easily enough space to accommodate two SIMs or a SIM and a microSD card, yet it only holds one SIM card. I might have accepted space constraints as an excuse if the SIM tray didn’t just have dead space built in.

Motorola includes facial recognition for sign-in. It also has a fingerprint scanner built into the power button, which makes it conveniently accessible whether using the phone folded open or closed.

Motorola has a bonus for creatives and handwriting enthusiasts. The Razr Fold supports a pressure-sensitive active stylus, and it worked quite well in my brief testing with it. I’d be careful about pushing too hard on the internal display, though. It’s also an optional accessory (i.e., even more money out of your pocket), and it doesn’t attach to the phone or charge from it either. It has its own separate charging sleeve that it inserts into for storage and recharging.

The speakers on the Razr Fold are decent, offering loud stereo sound that’s a decent match for the display.

Motorola has fitted a 5Gbps USB-C port with DisplayPort 1.2 output, letting the Razr Fold connect to an external display and work as something of a portable computer.

The Razr Fold is pricey, so it’s good to see that Motorola isn’t holding back on long-term support. The company is promising seven years of Android OS and security updates, which helps keep it competitive with Samsung and Google on those fronts.

The software itself is a tame implementation of Android. The phone came running Android 16, and it’s not heavy handed about AI features or bloated with unwanted software, though there is a button dedicated to recording notes, making images and quickly tapping into other AI features. The OS is fairly flexible with customization as well. I found the default quick setting buttons a little large, but the OS let me shrink some of them down. I could also go from a 4x6 home screen app grid to a 5x7 to get more apps just a tap away.

Motorola Razr Fold – Gaming and Performance

The Razr Fold doesn’t feature Qualcomm’s top-of-the-line chip, but it comes close with the Snapdragon 8 Gen 5, which gets 16GB of memory and 512GB of storage. This is a chip I saw in the OnePlus 15R , which mustered solid performance, and though the Razr Fold is wielding this chip in a much thinner chassis, it nearly keeps up. It’s not quite up to iPhone 17 or OnePlus 15 speeds, but it’s no slouch. The sustain is also impressive.

The phone performed surprisingly well for how thin it is. I played over a half hour of Neverness to Everness with the graphics settings at their max cinematic level, and though there was the occasional stutter, the game generally ran smoothly at 60FPS. At the end of my session, the phone wasn't even noticeably warm. It even managed 70% consistency in 3DMark’s Steel Nomad Light stress test.

The Razr Fold’s performance is enough to rival the Galaxy Z Fold 7 and even the new Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra despite the latter’s more advanced Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip. In my colleague Jackie’s review, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra could struggle under sustained loads. It started the Steel Nomad Light stress test with a high score of 1641 and sank down to 1,296 by the end of the 20-run gauntlet. That may have been more stable technically, but the Razr Fold started out higher at 2289 and finished with a low of 1600 points. It had also settled into a groove after 5 runs, so it seemed unlikely to ever sink as low as Samsung’s fold in the test.

The fact that Jackie found the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra uncomfortably warm to the touch after gaming while the Razr Fold was chilling puts the Razr in a great position to be the better gaming device.

The phone has a sizable 6,000mAh battery despite its thinness, and it’s even willing to take some pretty fast charging. It can juice back up at 80W from a wired connection of 50W from a wireless one. Sadly, even with some magnetism going on at the back of the phone, it doesn’t support Qi2. While battery life can vary dramatically from person to person, I was easily able to get through the day even while squeezing in some time gaming on the big screen.

Motorola didn’t skimp on the cameras included in the Razr Fold. It decked out the rear with a triple-sensor setup to rival Samsung, OnePlus, and Google, and it even has a couple of sharp selfie shooters. Here’s a quick rundown of what’s on deck:

50MP wide, f/1.6, 2.44-micron, 1/1.28”, OIS

50MP ultrawide, f/2.0, 1.28-micron, 1/2.76”

50MP telephoto, 3x optical zoom, f/2.4, 1.6-micron, 1/1.95, OIS

20MP exterior selfie, f/2.4, 1.22-micron, 90-degree FOV

32MP interior selfie, f/2.4, 1.28-micron, 88.5-degree FOV

I can’t say that the camera system is faultless, as it occasionally exhibits some oversharpening on the telephoto sensor, and it can get a bit soft and noisy in dimmer settings, but beyond those fairly common faults, it is excellent.

The cameras blend together well, matching one another’s color and dynamic range for a great consistency between shots. The sensors capture vivid color, bringing life to nature shots and street scenes alike. The cameras also snap sharp photos for loads of detail even when zooming in on them a bit. It’s just a bonus that the internal display’s squarer aspect ratio is all the better for previewing and reviewing the 3:2 photos that cameras will take.

The zoom is actually exceedingly strong. Though it has just a 3x optical, the 50MP sensor is happy to keep cropping in a bit further, and it has some impressive results. I could snap photos of details well beyond what I could see with my own eyes.

The sensors also do a great job handling macro shots, letting me get much closer to small subjects than I’m used to. The selfie sensors are no slouches either, snapping crisp photos with natural exposure. All of this combines to make the Razr Fold a rather excellent all around shooter for big and small subjects near and far.

The Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra may have added in some higher-end cameras for this generation, but it will likely have its work cut out for it beating the Razr Fold. Motorola included a bigger, higher-res telephoto sensor than the Z Fold 8 Ultra’s 10 megapixels, and the main sensor here may be lower resolution, but it’s offering a slightly wider aperture, bigger sensor, and bigger pixels.

articles.title: Naoki Hamaguchi Doubles Down on Connecting All Final Fantasy VII Spin-Offs Into Revelation’s Ending
articles.summary: Final Fantasy VII Revelation director Naoki Hamaguchi opened up on the game’s connection to the Advent Children film, saying that more than one of FF7’s spin-offs are going to tie into the game’s ending.
articles.body:
Final Fantasy VII Revelation director Naoki Hamaguchi opened up on the game’s connection to the Advent Children film, saying that more than one of FF7’s spin-offs are going to tie into the game’s ending.

In an interview with YouTuber Ashif’s Release Notes at Final Fantasy XIV Fan Festival Berlin 2026, Naoki revealed that he’s well aware of the fan theories surrounding the next game in the Remake trilogy, particularly where ties to other properties in the FF7 universe are concerned.

He assured Ashif that he’s carefully considering all of these titles, specifically mentioning Dirge of Cerberus , Crisis Core, and of course, the Advent Children movie.

Final Fantasy VII Revelation Screenshots

"I see a great deal of that discussion. I've seen a lot of people discussing and speculating off the back of interviews with myself and with Kitase-san, 'Is the ending of this going to connect to Advent Children?'” he began.

“But it's not a question. I don't want to sit here and say it connects to this, it connects to that. But obviously, there are a lot of other titles within the VII universe. So, we're talking about Advent Children, we're talking about Dirge of Cerberus, Crisis Core . And we want to bring all of those in and make sure we're not leaving those out.

“And then on top of that, once we have all of those in place, we're looking towards the ending. And then the question is, what kind of ending are we going to head for in Revelation that still has those ties? And I think that's something that I really hope players will look forward to finding out."

While Hamaguchi was careful not to say anything that would outright spoil things, his answer has certainly fueled an animated debate within the community, especially following similar comments previously made by other devs working on the Remake trilogy.

Hamaguchi made similar remarks in an August 1 interview with Automaton , confirming that the Remake series is a “new, overarching universe that encompasses the lore of the many various spin-offs” in the FF7 universe — “not just Advent Children, but also Dirge of Cerberus and Crisis Core.”

“We’re not denying the possibility of the ending tying into FFVII AC, but rather, we’re saying that FFVII AC has just been incorporated into the overarching FFVII remake series, including the ending. However, I won’t comment on whether the ending is positioned to lead into it,” he told the outlet.

And in 2023, producer Yoshinori Kitase told Eurogamer very definitely that this is the case: "We are finally going to link up with Advent Children, that is going to be part of canon," he said. "The overall storyline, the developments, will not go wildly out in a way that will not add up to Advent Children in the end. I don't think anyone wanted that, that's not what we're looking to create here.

"[But] to make sure it doesn't become stale and people know exactly where it's going, [that it] doesn't just follow the original word for word, we add in extra elements which add that little bit of doubt. Getting the right balance of that is so key. Ultimately, we're not trying to change the Final Fantasy 7 story into something really different. The overall balance wouldn't really allow for that anyway."

Hamaguchi’s latest comments have created stirred up a heated conversation within the fanbase, with some lamenting the trilogy’s shift away from the original game’s storyline in favor of a metaverse-style combo of all FF7 properties, while others remain cautiously optimistic about what this entails for the fates of Cloud, Tifa, Barret, and co.

In June, Hamaguchi spoke further about Revelation’s ending, saying that while players will be able to shape the story in some way, everyone will ultimately come to a "singular ending."

"The idea is to kind of change the approach and the depth of these story moments for these characters in this final chapter," he said. "We hope players look forward to that moment in the game."

Final Fantasy VII Revelation releases in spring 2027 on Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X and S, and PC via Steam and Epic Games Store.

Virginia (she/her) is IGN’s News Editor. With ten years of experience reporting on games and entertainment, she’s got a storied background in the fighting game community, influencer news, and viral online trends. Find her on Twitter at @TheeMissGlaze .

“And then on top of that, once we have all of those in place, we're looking towards the ending. And then the question is, what kind of ending are we going to head for in Revelation that still has those ties? And I think that's something that I really hope players will look forward to finding out."

While Hamaguchi was careful not to say anything that would outright spoil things, his answer has certainly fueled an animated debate within the community, especially following similar comments previously made by other devs working on the Remake trilogy.

Hamaguchi made similar remarks in an August 1 interview with Automaton , confirming that the Remake series is a “new, overarching universe that encompasses the lore of the many various spin-offs” in the FF7 universe — “not just Advent Children, but also Dirge of Cerberus and Crisis Core.”

“We’re not denying the possibility of the ending tying into FFVII AC, but rather, we’re saying that FFVII AC has just been incorporated into the overarching FFVII remake series, including the ending. However, I won’t comment on whether the ending is positioned to lead into it,” he told the outlet.

And in 2023, producer Yoshinori Kitase told Eurogamer very definitely that this is the case: "We are finally going to link up with Advent Children, that is going to be part of canon," he said. "The overall storyline, the developments, will not go wildly out in a way that will not add up to Advent Children in the end. I don't think anyone wanted that, that's not what we're looking to create here.

"[But] to make sure it doesn't become stale and people know exactly where it's going, [that it] doesn't just follow the original word for word, we add in extra elements which add that little bit of doubt. Getting the right balance of that is so key. Ultimately, we're not trying to change the Final Fantasy 7 story into something really different. The overall balance wouldn't really allow for that anyway."

Hamaguchi’s latest comments have created stirred up a heated conversation within the fanbase, with some lamenting the trilogy’s shift away from the original game’s storyline in favor of a metaverse-style combo of all FF7 properties, while others remain cautiously optimistic about what this entails for the fates of Cloud, Tifa, Barret, and co.
In June, Hamaguchi spoke further about Revelation’s ending, saying that while players will be able to shape the story in some way, everyone will ultimately come to a "singular ending."
"The idea is to kind of change the approach and the depth of these story moments for these characters in this final chapter," he said. "We hope players look forward to that moment in the game."
Final Fantasy VII Revelation releases in spring 2027 on Nintendo Switch 2, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X and S, and PC via Steam and Epic Games Store.

Virginia (she/her) is IGN’s News Editor. With ten years of experience reporting on games and entertainment, she’s got a storied background in the fighting game community, influencer news, and viral online trends. Find her on Twitter at @TheeMissGlaze .

articles.title: X-Men '97 Season 2's Penultimate Episode Features a Reunion We've Been Waiting For, But the Results Are Strangely Underwhelming
articles.summary: X-Men '97 Season 2, Episode 8 features a return fans have been waiting for, so why does it leave us feeling so cold? Read our full review of "Dead Man's Hand."
articles.body:
Warning: This review contains full spoilers for X-Men '97 Season 2, Episode 8!

I have to wonder if it was the smartest idea for the X-Men '97 crew to telegraph the resurrection of Gambit (A.J. LoCascio). At the time, that stinger scene was a great way to cap off Season 1 and tease what was to come. But now that we've finally arrived at Season 2, is having that knowledge working against the show as it actually brings Gambit back into play? All I can say for sure is that something is missing in Episode 8. Gambit's resurrection doesn't pack quite the emotional punch his death did back in 2024.

Maybe part of the problem is that we don't get a great sense of what Apocalypse's (Ross Marquand) larger goals are here. The obvious assumption was that he was assembling his latest and greatest team of Horsemen with which to dominate the world, and Gambit was his Death. But there's no indication that En Sabah Nur has been gathering other minions. He simply revived Gambit and then turned into a desiccated monkey corpse for some reason. I suppose we're meant to assume his spirit now resides within Gambit? Whatever the case, now back among the living, that simply leaves Gambit to assemble his old posse of thieves and assassins and do... whatever it is Apocalypse wanted him to do.

Part of that seems to involve punishing Candra, the X-Ternal to whom the two guilds have been paying their tithes for all these years. In what is easily the most disappointing element of Episode 8, we learn that Apocalypse and Candra were former lovers, and the latter stole a piece of his power before forsaking him. That all of this backstory is conveyed through a brief, matter-of-fact flashback sequence does this episode no favors at all. The Apocalypse/Candra dynamic needed to be a lot more fleshed out than it is, particularly with the previous foreshadowing in Episode 4.

Not to mention that, if the series really wants to dig into the concept of Apocalypse having a long-lost lover, the character Genesis holds far more storytelling potential. We can only hope this show sticks around long enough to tackle a proper House of X/Krakoa adaptation.

None of this is to say that Episode 8 doesn't sink its emotional hooks at times. While the long-awaited reunion between Rogue (Lenore Zann) and Gambit isn't quite what I hoped for, the two characters do have some strong scenes together. Rogue's opening nightmare is a strong start to the episode, and her entrance into Gambit and Xavier's (Marquand) psychic battle also stands out as one of the better moments of the episode. But again, too often throughout "Dead Man's Hand," I was left with the feeling that something is missing.

It's telling that I wound up finding more weight in the Summers family drama than Gambit's return. Episode 8 makes the most of the fleeting alliance between the X-Men and Cable's (Chris Potter) team, along with all the awkwardness that comes from father and mother being reunited with their now much older son. That plays right into Cable's more ruthless nature and his struggle to still be the man his parents (briefly) raised him to be. The Summers family tree is so stupid and so convoluted, but somehow this series makes us care about all of it.

It's also fun seeing the X-Men fully reunited after spending nearly all the season split into different camps. There's a small part of my fanboy brain that dislikes seeing the team simultaneously decked out in a mixture of classic '80s costumes and more modern New X-Men suits, but I'll allow it. In what is definitely the highlight of Episode 8, we see the combined might of the X-Men and X-Force take on Gambit's forces, only to get absolutely wrecked by Nightcrawler (Adrian Hough). It's a blast seeing what happens when this normally benevolent hero finally cuts loose.

"Dead Man's Hand" certainly has its moments, but this episode doesn't come together as well as I would've liked. And that's a little worrisome now that we only have one chapter left in Season 2. The show has an awful lot of ground to cover in terms of reestablishing Apocalypse in the present and orchestrating this final showdown between rival mutant teams. As strong as Season 2 has generally been, it would be a huge shame for it to collapse at the finish line.

articles.title: Big Walk Is Unlike Any Other Co-op Game Around, Pushing You to Solve Clever Puzzles With Your Friends by Truly Working Together
articles.summary: A clever co-op puzzle adventure that uses communication like no other.
articles.body:
To know something's name is to understand it — at least just a little, be it the thing itself, or the world around it. In Big Walk, there are lots of things yet unnamed. You will certainly recognize trees, mountains, that dang cowbell. But there are plenty of things you won’t: the red, peanut-shaped objects my group calls a bean, which makes the structures they must be delivered to the bean towers. To us, the underground tunnel system is the backrooms, and the glowing medicine balls that light paths throughout the world are simply orbs – but not to be confused with the Big Orb, a mysterious and ominous structure looming in the distance. Big Walk is a co-op-only puzzle adventure that relies heavily on shared experience, shared language. Its genius lies in how it pushes you to decipher the logic behind the clever puzzles spread around its open world in a way that only you and your companions will understand. With all the twists and limitations it imposes, it’s unlike any other multiplayer game out there.

Big Walk is a puzzle game, and the puzzle is communication. Everyone is initially dropped into a playground of sorts with some colorful, blocklike structures to climb on, light switches to flip, and your controls pinned up as posters. I call this place home. Crucially, you are given no objective. We fiddle about with the buttons, obnoxiously clang the cowbell. We test out our movement options – mostly arm gestures – by looking at our shadows. Eventually, we head out into a lifelike world with lush foliage and waves breaking on the beach; it's a direct contrast to our charming, goofy characters, who are, essentially, a stack of three colored balls with googly eyes, stick arms, and twig legs (and a nose that moves like a mouth as we speak in-game).

When someone asked what we're supposed to do, what the objective of this game was, I couldn’t really answer that. And so we walked. But here's what I knew at this point: Big Walk has walking and puzzles. That, and outside of arm flailing or typing out written messages, we can only communicate through proximity-based voice chat. This means your voice is muffled when you're behind a wall, and echoes when you're in a vast tunnel. If someone wanders too far off, I can no longer hear them, and as a game that can only be played with others, it’s “cooperative” in the very sense of the term. There's no way to play Big Walk alone, and it supports up to 12 players with different settings for different sized groups: two, three, or four-plus, which adjusts puzzles slightly to suit the number of people in a session. Big Walk cleverly takes advantage of the essential limitation of proximity chat, and it wouldn't be the same without it.

Venturing out, my group of three walks together along desert terrain and up a cliffside until we find a button on a platform. We originally think nothing happens when it's pushed, but someone notices a faint red light flashing in the distance. It illuminates each time it's pressed, so we send someone in its direction to see what’s out there. There's a red bean in a box, which opens when the button is pushed. He grabs it and rushes back. No one knows what to do with it but it seems important, so we hold onto it (or try our best until someone drops it while falling off a cliff). Through that simple opening task, we start to get it: This puzzle, this bean, they’re teaching us something about the world and what we need to do within it. We're starting to create our own language.

Each piece of this map is cleverly designed to nudge your group to build something together, forms of communication that feel like only you understand. We keep walking, keep exploring and finding puzzles that require real teamwork, and continue to build our language. My group played in several sessions across a few days: a core group of three, with some stragglers jumping in here and there. We spent nearly 20 delightful hours romping around. It's easy for people to jump in and out of the session, popping in to adventure for a bit. There is a kink in this system, though. The save file is tied to the player who originally hosted the game. For my group, that was me. If my companions wanted to play when I wasn't there, they'd have to start a new save file—and a new big walk. This may very well be by design; developer House House wants a group to stick together. But I felt bad when someone wanted to play, but I couldn't.

Big Walk's world runs on a day-night cycle, with sun-soaked days and pitch-dark nights. And in the latter, a different kind of communication is built. Early on, my friend Riley dropped our only flashlight off a cliff, immediately after I accidentally kicked our walkie-talkie down the same one. We spent a not-insignificant amount of time looking for our tools because, without them, we could easily lose each other in the dead of night. (Even more so when looking for Riley, who got stuck in a hole while searching for our gear). Perhaps in another game, losing your tools or falling in a ditch would be frustrating. Not so here. While movement can be finicky at times, and you will briefly get stuck in spots, Big Walk often felt even more impactful when things were going very, very wrong.

We spent plenty of time doing Big Walk's actual puzzles, which are scattered around the map and usually embedded in big, brightly colored structures: a green horror movie house, an orange colosseum, a blue sound stage. Some of them are relatively easy, like throwing an orb into a basketball hoop multiple times, or playing a game of telephone to identify a specific sequence of shapes or buttons to push. But there are mechanical challenges as well, ones that require platforming and precise movement or throws. There's an entertaining puzzle that requires one person to put on a blindfold (which is actually a big, weird gold head that blocks their view) and navigate through an obstacle course. The others then have to yell instructions at them about where to go and what to do; the scariest part of this was figuring out how to time a jump over a gap. These challenges don't necessarily get progressively harder, because you're free to do whichever puzzle in whatever order you discover them. Some are certainly difficult, but never cruelly so. Big Walk always gives you the tools you need to solve them, so there's no danger of a dramatic learning curve.

One particularly inventive puzzle had my friend Chris locked in a soundproof room trying to relay little musical jingles to us so we could match that to stereos playing the corresponding melodies. Another forced us to split up onto three platforms that were pretty far away from each other and correctly time a synchronized button push. There are a couple puzzles with similar ideas, and the problem was often that we only had two walkie-talkies amongst us. So, we used our laser pointer to signify a countdown or our arms to send a silent message. Little by little, we created a sort of body language cipher to help solve matching puzzles and timing-based challenges alike, and it was a thrill to naturally develop our own system of visual cues.

Each of these puzzles rewards us with another red bean we have to take care of as we bring it back to a bean tower for deposit. Once you've found enough beans for a given tower, you get a special key to unlock something new and helpful: stuff you otherwise couldn't figure out how to operate, like a stalled train or an island-spanning chair lift. And in this progression, Big Walk further embeds the ethos that these discoveries are yours to make.

Big Walk's puzzles are always sharp, and always fun. The use of proximity chat makes the process of solving them feel special in a way I haven’t experienced in a game for a long time. Despite the recent wave of co-op games with an emphasis on hanging out with your friends, it feels so new to play in this particular way, as if we were all physically in this virtual space together. Video games often make us feel like superheroes, like the world revolves around our individual characters. In Big Walk, relationships and language are that superpower. The world doesn't revolve around me, but us .

So much of Big Walk's fun is found in the spaces between the puzzles, too. One of my favorite moments was this time Riley and I wandered away from Chris to go gallivanting in nature without care. This would not have been a big deal… if Riley and I did not have both walkie-talkies. Notoriously bad at navigating, we got wildly lost, even more so after we tumbled down the mountains once again. We were lost for nearly an hour, maybe longer. We went to the train to honk its horn. We tried to follow the coastline, then the train line itself, to make our way back to the place where we first realized we'd lost Chris. Then, a flare shot up in the distance. We walked toward the sound and eventually the direction of the green hue the blast gave off. That's where we found him, at a bean puzzle, firing off flares. Eventually, we sent Chris off to follow the curve of the flare and the bean was waiting at the end of it, like a pot of gold at the end of a rainbow. Riley and I certainly couldn't have been trusted to go find it.

I spent a lot of time playing Big Walk over the last week, but I also spent a lot of time thinking about it, and talking about it with the folks I played with. I'm thinking a lot about names, and the power they hold. In the book Braiding Sweetgrass: Indigenous Wisdom, Scientific Knowledge, and the Teachings of Plants , author and scientist Robin Wall Kimmerer writes that names are how we, as humans, build relationships with each other and "the living world." She muses on what it might be like to not know the names of things around you. Kimmerer writes, "I think it would be a little scary and disorienting – like being lost in a foreign city where you can’t read the street signs." Big Walk's opening feels a little bit like that. Its island is not yet a place with which we've built a relationship, or developed a language. The moment you understand this, Big Walk changes. And what a special thing it is to name this world with friends.

articles.title: House of the Dragon's Season 3 Finale Had Little Sense of an Ending... But a Spectacular Battle That Leaves Everything in Play for the Last Season
articles.summary: House of the Dragon Season 3 Finale Recap and Review: There’s little sense of an ending here, but this spectacular battle left everything to play for in the final season.
articles.body:
Full spoilers follow for House of the Dragon Season 3, Episode 8, “The Traitors of Tumbleton.”

Back in the day, Game of Thrones typically delivered its big action beats in a season’s penultimate episode and spent the finale wrapping up loose ends and setting the stakes for the following year . House of the Dragon is a different beast: this season began and ended with all-out war, and if anything, this finale leaves too many loose ends dangling. If it’s less punch-the-air satisfying than the season opener, it may have more consequential revelations for what’s to come.

In King’s Landing, Rhaenyra (Emma D’Arcy) continues to make one unforced error after another. Driven to near hysteria by the news that Aegon (Tom Glynn-Carney) has survived, she exiles one of her more clear-eyed advisers, Mysaria (Sonoya Mizuno) and baffles her subjects, speaking to them about prophecies – occasionally in High Valyrian – when they’re worried about putting food on the table.

More troublingly, she makes a classic Henry II of England error and has the head of her church assassinated in his cathedral. That didn’t go well for Henry, who sparked widespread unrest and had to make significant concessions to the Pope to settle things down, and doesn’t seem likely to go well for Rhaenyra either. Perhaps significantly, Rhaenyra has the generally likeable Alyn (Abubakar Salim) strike the fatal blow. His brother Addam (Clinton Liberty) accused him of being overly ambitious and under Rhaenyra’s thumb; he may have had a point. Rhaenyra is no longer as hesitant as she once was, but fear has also made her vicious. The woman who hisses commands to Alyn in the Sept is not the same one who wrung her hands over violence last season. Something has broken in her; she may no longer be one of the Targaryens capable of greatness.

We also bade farewell this week to Queen Helaena (Phia Saban) , who has given one of the most quietly and consistently compelling performances this season as a woman who knows how tragically it’s all going to play out. The manner of her death – she threw herself out a window – was the same as the book, but there are some differences: her youngest son, Maelor, was born before her death on the page, and met his own tragic end. This is less horrible than the murder of an infant might have been, but it’s plenty disturbing. Her final scenes with Rhaenyra are also superbly done: watch how Viserys’ older daughter, when she tries to force Helaena to eat, impatiently puts aside the very tapestry that might have given her the answers she so desperately sought.

At Harrenhal, Aegon arrives on Sunfyre and resolves to work together with his wayward brother Aemond (Ewan Mitchell) for maybe the first time in their lives – albeit not before slapping him around a bit and threatening to kill him for, in fairness, his attempt on Aegon’s life. But Aemond’s obvious guilt and true repentance saves him; the pair set off to find the still-missing Vhagar and take the fight to Rhaenyra. We also learn, by the way, that Alys Rivers (Gayle Rankin) is the former Lady of Harrenhal. She was the wife of Black Harren, its builder, and was cursed to remain in the limits of its lands and never die when she sought dark powers in the forest to save the life of her badly-burned son. Alys’ background was never established fully in the book, so this is a new and potentially pretty potent wrinkle. In fact, Aegon and Aemond’s reconciliation is also new territory, and it’s going to be interesting to see how much trouble that terrible twosome get into as a united front.

The majority of the episode, however, concerns the attack on Tumbleton. Despite the efforts of the late Ser Criston Cole (Fabien Frankel) , the Rivermen have arrived en masse and Daemon Targaryen (Matt Smith) has flown down on Caraxes to take command and, oh yes, flame anyone who needs flamed. Ser Gwayne Hightower (Freddie Fox), one of the most likeable characters on the board and therefore probably doomed, tries to make peace by offering the return of the imprisoned Corlys Velaryon (Steve Toussaint), but no dice. He and Daeron (Benjamin Evan Ainsworth) are left trying to survive in the besieged city; it’s not clear by the end of the episode that Daeron is OK.

Meanwhile, Ormund is searching desperately for his ace in the hole, the dragonrider Ulf (Tom Bennett), who is so excited about his heel turn that he’s drunk himself into a stupor. Here, Ormund makes an ultimately fatal mistake. He’s so overcome by the stink of the privy where he finally discovers Ulf that he entirely loses his temper and whales on the other man. Ulf still does his bidding long enough to flame half the army of Rivermen – but he then turns his fury, and Silverwing, on Tumbleton itself and Ormund in particular. So long, you prissy little manbaby bully.

Ulf is not the only dragonrider who’s in trouble this week: Hugh (Kieran Bew) also left his post in King’s Landing to look for his wife in Tumbleton, running in with the ground forces, while Baela (Bethany Antonia) is grounded in the Keep after daring to criticise Rhaenyra. As for the episode’s title, there are any number of candidates. Ulf obviously, but Hugh also disobeys orders to go to Tumbleton. Daeron and Gwayne both betray Ormund in attempting to sue for peace; Ormund has arguably betrayed Aegon in elevating Daeron. And Daemon accuses Corlys of treachery when he argues for peace. There’s a lot of it going around.

The end result is shellshocked troops stumbling around a charred battlefield, trying to collect corpses, while Caraxes and Hugh’s Vermithor chase off Ulf’s Silverwing. The Battle of Tumbleton is – at best – a draw for the Blacks, and if it’s a victory for the Greens it might prove to be a Pyrrhic one, what with the loss of Ormund, their best strategist, and the uncertain fate of Ulf and Silverwing afterwards.

House of the Dragon: Season 3 Official Images

At this point it’s a positive disadvantage to have read the books; some of us have been waiting for one face-off for nearly half a decade now, since that could plausibly have happened at the end of Season 1 or the start of Season 2. Now we will have to wait two more years if it’s even going to happen as written. The overall shape of the show is also becoming more evident, and something that I wrote about last season seems to be taking shape ( read that here if you’re not scared of major spoilers ). Whether showrunner Ryan Condal and his team can stick the landing for the finale better than Game of Thrones did remains to be seen, but they have made a great foundation for it this year.

articles.title: Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls Ticks Nearly Every Box, With Gorgeous Art and Excellent Action That Can Appeal to Players of Any Skill Level
articles.summary: A gorgeous and innovative fighting game that can appeal to all skill levels.
articles.body:
It’s a very rare feat when a fighting game manages to tick virtually every box across the board: Excellent fighting mechanics, fantastic teaching tools, great netcode, and both hardcore extras like Replay Takeover alongside more casual treats like a worthwhile story and ancillary modes. Marvel Tokon: Fighting Souls is about as close as a game has gotten to checking all of those boxes since Street Fighter 6. This is a gorgeous and innovative fighting game that can appeal to players of all skill levels, with characters that are easy and satisfying to just mash some buttons with, but equally fun to dive deep into and tinker with in the lab. The albatross that used to hang around its neck was the poor performance of the PC version at launch, but thanks to a recent patch that seems to have fixed most of those issues, Tokon is now a recommendation I can make wholeheartedly without any caveats.

Let’s start with the fundamentals: Tokon is a 4v4 tag fighter with a bunch of unique rules that attempt to control the inherent chaos of having eight swappable characters in a single match. For example, all characters on a team share the same lifebar, removing one of the core elements of traditional tag fighting games, which typically let you swap in a fresh fighter so the damaged one can restore health while they sit on the sidelines. It’s a smart adjustment that allows for a much cleaner UI, avoids the pitfall of 4v4 matches that would otherwise run too long, and removes one of the big barriers of entry to any traditional tag fighter: the need to learn multiple characters in order to have a competitive team.

But what’s especially cool is that while you can be very strong by knowing how to play just one character, there’s still a ton of value in crafting a well-synergized team. For instance, if you know that your main struggles in a particular match up, like maybe your opponent plays Magneto and you would have trouble against his strong zoning, you could have a better option waiting in the wings. Or maybe you have a character that you really like but have trouble opening opponents up with, like in my case, Blade – you could lead with a more mix-up-heavy character, and once you land the hit, swap to continue the combo and deal more damage than the mix-up character might have been able to get on their own.

What I really love about this system is that you can add new elements to your gameplan piece-by-piece rather than feeling like you need to have everything on lock right from the start. When I first started playing, all I needed to do was get competent with Spider-Man. I learned some high/low mix-up options, some bread and butter combos, got a basic understanding of how to use his web-zip to maneuver around the screen, and I felt ready to start playing against other people online. When I started to feel like I hit the ceiling of what I could do with just Spider-Man, I went back into training mode to learn more about Blade, and was able to add new layers to my gameplan. After that, I added in Magneto as an assist to help me convert more damage off of the low part of my high/low mix-up. Now I’m experimenting with the fourth position to try to find someone else with an assist that adds extra value to my team. This process of being able to start with a small foundation and build upon it is the ideal way to learn a fighting game, and Tokon feels designed specifically for it.

Those assists are where things start to get a little strange. You see, Tokon doesn’t begin as a 4v4 fighter. Instead, every match starts with just two of the characters on each team available, with the remaining fighters needing to be unlocked by either landing a light auto-combo, hitting the opponent with a move near the corner that causes a stage transition or wallsplat, or losing a round. Unlocking these characters is important, because each one increases your overall health and adds another bar to your Assemble meter, which governs the ability to call assists during specific moments.

Tokon has a lot of hyper specific rules surrounding its assists, which leads to a system that can be fairly overwhelming for newcomers – it was certainly a lot to take in for me, even as someone who’s played many tag fighters like Marvel vs Capcom, Dragon Ball FighterZ , 2XKO , and more. Before a match begins, you place your four characters into various positions: Leader, Shooter, Vertical, and Assault. These placements determine what kind of assist is used when you call them out in neutral (meaning when you’re just standing still or walking without pressing a button or blocking). Leader is whoever the current point character is, Shooters will use a projectile, Verticals predictably cover a vertical hit box, and the Assault spot is generally reserved for each character’s most powerful assist.

These neutral assists don’t cost any meter, but if you try to call an assist after landing an attack to pick up a combo or to cover your recovery after a blocked move, you’ll instead get a universal dash-attack assist that costs one bar of the Assemble meter. What’s finicky about this system is that you have to be very precise with your assist call, because if it happens too early (or too late) the assist won’t come out. This extends to the active tag system, which allows you to switch control to your assist character for a brief period while they’re on the screen. It’s very similar to 2XKO, but here it feels much more restrained. In 2XKO, you can basically swap to your assist character at any point, enabling some really tricky mix-up opportunities. Tokon, on the other hand, seems to be much more hesitant to allow these kinds of unrestrained mix-ups. That isn’t to say that you can’t do gnarly things with the active tag system once you lock your opponent down in blockstun, just that the rules that govern the system are a little more rigid than what I’m used to.

And you know what, that’s probably for a good reason – given how cluttered the screen can get with four characters throwing nonsense out all at once, I think the amount of chaos that Tokon allows is already more than enough. Especially when you’ve got characters like Peni Parker, who takes up a huge portion of the screen and can send out a bunch of random drones; Magneto, who can fill the screen with literal garbage that can enhance his attacks; Magik, who can summon fire pillars that cover a fourth of the field. It can be very easy to lose track of what’s going on.

There are some cool nuances to the tag system as well: The raw tag outs have a bit of delay to them, so you can do cool stuff like tag, perform a move during the delay, and when you take control of the incoming character, the previous character’s move will cover your approach without needing to spend a bar of the assemble meter. It’s touches like these that really add that extra layer of depth that makes learning Tokon on a deeper level so much fun.

The characters themselves are Tokon’s greatest strength. We’re no stranger to seeing a lot of these faces in fighting games before, but ArcSystem Works has gone above and beyond in terms of making them feel authentic to their comic book counterparts, while also ensuring they are each a blast to play in their own particular way. Spidey is able to zip all across the stage, baiting anti-airs by hanging and then jumping off his webs; Storm can manipulate the weather to push and pull objects and enemies (or even snatch her opponent in a command grab from half-a-screen away with a gust of wind that pushes her forward); Deadpool is a walking love letter to the FGC with a kit that is almost entirely comprised of memes and special moves from Street Fighter, Mortal Kombat, King of Fighters, Tekken, Guilty Gear, and much, much more.

It’s an impressive roster of 21, and while there are certainly some notable omissions (especially on the X-Men front) and curious inclusions ( *cough Danger cough* ), the characters who did make the cut do a good job of justifying their spot with very unique playstyles that add something special to the roster. I can’t imagine Green Goblin being at the top of anyone’s list of characters to include in a Marvel fighting game, but he has ended up being one of the most interesting thanks to his unique ability to fight both on and off his glider.

The most delightful surprise about Tokon is that its story mode is actually pretty dang good! It’s broken up into five episodes, with each episode essentially being its own graphic novel centered around one of the five canonical teams of four: The Fighting Avengers, The Unbreakable X-Men, The Amazing Guardians, Samurai Outriders, and Knights of Doom.

The set up for all of this in-fighting between Marvel heroes and anti-heroes (and a few straight up villains) is the same throughout each of the episodes: an otherworldly being known as The Champion has challenged five of the Earth’s mightiest warriors to compete in a tournament, with the winners getting the opportunity to do battle with him – and, should they win, he will grant them any wish they desire. So it’s basically a Marvel version of Mortal Kombat meets Twisted Metal, and while that concept doesn’t win any points for creativity, it does for execution.

The episodes themselves are presented like motion comics, each illustrated by a different famous manga or comic book artist. This gives each story its own distinct art style, and I loved seeing all the different takes on these iconic characters. It’s especially cool as a big anime fan to see famous mangaka like Hiro Mashima of Fairy Tail fame and Betten Court, the creator of My Hero Academia: Vigilantes, each apply their very distinctive art styles to classic Marvel characters like Captain America and Spider-Man.

It’s not just the art though, the writing is strong as well. Kieron Gillen, the writer of all five mini-stories, does a great job of tailoring each one to the strengths of the characters involved. The Amazing Guardians focuses on Peter Parker struggling with the need to be a leader and reluctant mentor to Ms. Marvel, while also trying to rein in the added chaos of having a wildcard like Peter Quill on his team. Meanwhile, the Unbreakable X-Men episode deals with the familiar conflict of Storm, Magik, and Wolverine being heroes to a population that reviles them purely because they’re mutants. There’s not a lot of time to explore these themes beyond anything but a surface level, but the fact that there’s at least something to chew on at all is a step in the right direction for fighting game stories.

These episodes aren’t the end of Tokon’s ancillary modes either. There’s a survival mode that challenges you to take on 100 fights against steadily more difficult foes, giving you a variety of stat boosts to choose from as you increase your power level every five rounds. Your progress is saved at those five-round milestones as well, so it isn’t a true survival mode, since you get to restart without losing much progress, but it’s still a nice diversion for people who want another challenge to conquer before taking the fight online.

And then there’s Arcadia Rumble, which is entirely its own beast. It’s almost structured like a fighting game version of the City Trial mode from Kirby Air Riders , in that it’s split up into two phases that alternate for a total of five rounds, with the first phase being all about powering up your characters, and the second phase being about taking your powered up characters and competing against other juiced up fighters. Up to eight players and their customizable avatars roam around Tokon’s gigantic lobby with the goal of collecting stars. Stars can be obtained by beating up other players and knocking them out, participating in limited time events that pop up around the map, or defeating other players in the second phase, which are the traditional 4v4 battles. It’s actually pretty fun, and while I don’t see myself personally spending a ton of time with it beyond what I’ve played for this review, I can definitely see its value as a mode where players of all skill levels can play together and still have a chance to win.

This whole package is rounded out with some of the best teaching tools I’ve seen in a fighting game: General mechanics breakdown with playable lessons, character guides that explain the basics of each kit, practical combo explainers that cover things like how to convert a combo off of a unique skill, and my favorite feature, free-form combo challenges that simply give you a move you need to include in the combo and a damage threshold you need to hit.

I love this so much, because it really encourages people to actually experiment and learn the characters rather than just memorize a string of buttons. The prompts you’re given are often very practical as well, teaching me how I should combo off of Spider-Man’s overhead, or what I should do when I land a hit but don’t have any assemble meter, or what my big cashout combo is when I land a hit and have full resources. Not to mention the excellent training mode, replay searching, replay takeovers, training presets, and so on. It’s everything I could ask for when it comes to learning tools, and Tokon has it all right out of the gate.

I’d be remiss not to mention the PC performance woes that many people have had since launch, and even in the beta before it. Personally, I didn’t actually have any notable issues on my rig, but I say that as someone running a GeForce RTX 5090 and AMD Ryzen 9 16-Core processor with 32 GBs of RAM, so I would certainly hope that’s the case.

That said, on several occasions while I was playing online this past weekend, I’d be in a match where everything moved at a fraction of the normal speed. These games always were against other PC players who had green network connections when I accepted the match, and they felt very different from the standard experience of playing someone on a poor connection. My guess is that these opponents were having performance issues, and that those problems were affecting my game even if I wasn’t personally experiencing them.

But wait! Good news arrived just as I was finishing up this review: A patch dropped only a few days after release that has seemingly fixed many of the PC issues that were being reported. True enough, since then I haven’t seen any matches like what I just described. I haven’t done a ton of testing myself yet, so I’ll continue to play on PC and will update this review should any issues arise, but it seems like the Tokon team may have managed to narrowly avert disaster.

However, the one minor complaint I do still have regarding online play is the fact that matchmaking has been quite slow considering how many players Tokon has. The speed of getting in and out of matches is the one place Tokon pales in comparison to other modern fighters, which is a bit of a bummer. But since you can mess around in training mode during a queue, it’s at least more time that I get to spend working on my combos, and I certainly need the practice.
