We’re no stranger to seeing a lot of these faces in fighting games before, but ArcSystem Works has gone above and beyond in terms of making them feel authentic to their comic book counterparts, while also ensuring they are each a blast to play in their own particular way. Spidey is able to zip all across the stage, baiting anti-airs by hanging and then jumping off his webs; Storm can manipulate the weather to push and pull objects and enemies (or even snatch her opponent in a command grab from half-a-screen away with a gust of wind that pushes her forward); Deadpool is a walking love letter to the FGC with a kit that is almost entirely comprised of memes and special moves from Street Fighter, Mortal Kombat, King of Fighters, Tekken, Guilty Gear, and much, much more.

It’s an impressive roster of 21, and while there are certainly some notable omissions (especially on the X-Men front) and curious inclusions ( *cough Danger cough* ), the characters who did make the cut do a good job of justifying their spot with very unique playstyles that add something special to the roster. I can’t imagine Green Goblin being at the top of anyone’s list of characters to include in a Marvel fighting game, but he has ended up being one of the most interesting thanks to his unique ability to fight both on and off his glider.

The most delightful surprise about Tokon is that its story mode is actually pretty dang good! It’s broken up into five episodes, with each episode essentially being its own graphic novel centered around one of the five canonical teams of four: The Fighting Avengers, The Unbreakable X-Men, The Amazing Guardians, Samurai Outriders, and Knights of Doom.

The set up for all of this in-fighting between Marvel heroes and anti-heroes (and a few straight up villains) is the same throughout each of the episodes: an otherworldly being known as The Champion has challenged five of the Earth’s mightiest warriors to compete in a tournament, with the winners getting the opportunity to do battle with him – and, should they win, he will grant them any wish they desire. So it’s basically a Marvel version of Mortal Kombat meets Twisted Metal, and while that concept doesn’t win any points for creativity, it does for execution.

The episodes themselves are presented like motion comics, each illustrated by a different famous manga or comic book artist. This gives each story its own distinct art style, and I loved seeing all the different takes on these iconic characters. It’s especially cool as a big anime fan to see famous mangaka like Hiro Mashima of Fairy Tail fame and Betten Court, the creator of My Hero Academia: Vigilantes, each apply their very distinctive art styles to classic Marvel characters like Captain America and Spider-Man.

It’s not just the art though, the writing is strong as well. Kieron Gillen, the writer of all five mini-stories, does a great job of tailoring each one to the strengths of the characters involved. The Amazing Guardians focuses on Peter Parker struggling with the need to be a leader and reluctant mentor to Ms. Marvel, while also trying to rein in the added chaos of having a wildcard like Peter Quill on his team. Meanwhile, the Unbreakable X-Men episode deals with the familiar conflict of Storm, Magik, and Wolverine being heroes to a population that reviles them purely because they’re mutants. There’s not a lot of time to explore these themes beyond anything but a surface level, but the fact that there’s at least something to chew on at all is a step in the right direction for fighting game stories.

These episodes aren’t the end of Tokon’s ancillary modes either. There’s a survival mode that challenges you to take on 100 fights against steadily more difficult foes, giving you a variety of stat boosts to choose from as you increase your power level every five rounds. Your progress is saved at those five-round milestones as well, so it isn’t a true survival mode, since you get to restart without losing much progress, but it’s still a nice diversion for people who want another challenge to conquer before taking the fight online.

And then there’s Arcadia Rumble, which is entirely its own beast. It’s almost structured like a fighting game version of the City Trial mode from Kirby Air Riders , in that it’s split up into two phases that alternate for a total of five rounds, with the first phase being all about powering up your characters, and the second phase being about taking your powered up characters and competing against other juiced up fighters. Up to eight players and their customizable avatars roam around Tokon’s gigantic lobby with the goal of collecting stars. Stars can be obtained by beating up other players and knocking them out, participating in limited time events that pop up around the map, or defeating other players in the second phase, which are the traditional 4v4 battles. It’s actually pretty fun, and while I don’t see myself personally spending a ton of time with it beyond what I’ve played for this review, I can definitely see its value as a mode where players of all skill levels can play together and still have a chance to win.

This whole package is rounded out with some of the best teaching tools I’ve seen in a fighting game: General mechanics breakdown with playable lessons, character guides that explain the basics of each kit, practical combo explainers that cover things like how to convert a combo off of a unique skill, and my favorite feature, free-form combo challenges that simply give you a move you need to include in the combo and a damage threshold you need to hit.

I love this so much, because it really encourages people to actually experiment and learn the characters rather than just memorize a string of buttons. The prompts you’re given are often very practical as well, teaching me how I should combo off of Spider-Man’s overhead, or what I should do when I land a hit but don’t have any assemble meter, or what my big cashout combo is when I land a hit and have full resources. Not to mention the excellent training mode, replay searching, replay takeovers, training presets, and so on. It’s everything I could ask for when it comes to learning tools, and Tokon has it all right out of the gate.

I’d be remiss not to mention the PC performance woes that many people have had since launch, and even in the beta before it. Personally, I didn’t actually have any notable issues on my rig, but I say that as someone running a GeForce RTX 5090 and AMD Ryzen 9 16-Core processor with 32 GBs of RAM, so I would certainly hope that’s the case.

That said, on several occasions while I was playing online this past weekend, I’d be in a match where everything moved at a fraction of the normal speed. These games always were against other PC players who had green network connections when I accepted the match, and they felt very different from the standard experience of playing someone on a poor connection. My guess is that these opponents were having performance issues, and that those problems were affecting my game even if I wasn’t personally experiencing them.

But wait! Good news arrived just as I was finishing up this review: A patch dropped only a few days after release that has seemingly fixed many of the PC issues that were being reported. True enough, since then I haven’t seen any matches like what I just described. I haven’t done a ton of testing myself yet, so I’ll continue to play on PC and will update this review should any issues arise, but it seems like the Tokon team may have managed to narrowly avert disaster.

However, the one minor complaint I do still have regarding online play is the fact that matchmaking has been quite slow considering how many players Tokon has. The speed of getting in and out of matches is the one place Tokon pales in comparison to other modern fighters, which is a bit of a bummer. But since you can mess around in training mode during a queue, it’s at least more time that I get to spend working on my combos, and I certainly need the practice.

articles.title: The Voice of The Witcher's Geralt Says He'd Sue Every Single AI Platform With His Voice on It 'Into the Ground' if He Could
articles.summary: Doug Cockle, the voice behind The Witcher’s Geralt, has hit out at AI platforms that feature his voice, saying he’d sue them if he could.
articles.body:
Doug Cockle, the voice behind The Witcher’s Geralt, has hit out at AI platforms that feature his voice, saying he’d sue them if he could.

Speaking to Polygon , Cockle called AI replications of his voice “the bugbear of my life,” and expressed concern at the technology being used to make Geralt say awful things, which might then mislead some into thinking Cockle had actually provided the voice.

“If I had the power, the money, and the influence, I would sue every single AI platform out there with my voice on it. I would sue them into the ground,” he said.

“More than money or anything else is that they could make Geralt say horrible things. They could make Geralt a racist. They could make him a misogynist. They could make him have political views that are absolutely horrific.

“I’m being a little bit passionate about this, but it is the bugbear of my life at the moment. There are people behind these voices. They’re not just digital imprints.”

Cockle has been a vocal critic of generative AI, telling IGN in 2023 that he was worried about people using it for nefarious purposes .

"AI is inevitable and developers will use AI. We are not 100% sure exactly what that means," Cockle said at the time. "They're already doing it in various ways, filling in background, NPC voices, and things like that, which is unfortunate because those voices were all human beings at one point, and the voices are all modelled on human beings. So they have taken someone's voice, put it into their database, digitized it and are using it to say things that the individual never said. There's something unethical about that and so there's a lot of debate going on."

Cockle was contacted by an AI company a few years ago who wanted to upload his Geralt voice to its database. "And I said no, and I still say no. But that's not because I don't like AI," he said.

"It's because I think with voice actors, particularly with voice actors who do main character roles, it is a reality that people are ripping our voices off. That's happening. It's happened to me on multiple occasions. I can't even police it because I would spend all my time policing this stupid stuff."

Even if people are using the voice with good intentions, like genuine fans making Witcher mods , it directly impacts voice actors, Cockle added. "Every time somebody does that, they're effectively robbing me of income, and not just me, any other voice actor who they do it with. We're all watching our voices get used in ways that we would rather they weren't."

It's when those using AI do have illicit purposes that it gets really scary though. "This is the bit that we really don't like about AI, is that if they can do it for things that are just commercially questionable, then they can do it with things that are politically or ethically bad," Cockle said.

"Somebody could use AI to produce something racist using Geralt's voice, using my voice, or just something against anything that most normal people think is good. That's where the AI gets dangerous. Fake news, false news, false opinions. We're seeing it with politicians now. People are putting things out there. So AI is not the problem. It's the people using AI."

Cockle continued: "It's changed a lot as well, because when The Witcher 3 came out, I don't think that people playing games, not that they weren't interested, but they didn't really think about who was voicing these characters. It wasn't something that was of great interest. But I've watched over the years, it has become more and more interesting to players and to fans who the people are behind these voices, and that's a fantastic thing. But it also means that those voices are much more personalized. It's not just Geralt. That is my voice."

Video game voice actors previously called out AI-generated explicit Skyrim mods , and Assassin's Creed Syndicate voice actress Victoria Atkin called AI-generated mods the “invisible enemy we're fighting right now” after discovering her voice was used by cloning software. Paul Eiding, the voice actor behind Colonel Campbell in the Metal Gear Solid series, also condemned its use .

The issue was raised again today when it emerged that Saber Interactive, the company behind Warhammer 40,000: Space Marine 2, had used ChatGPT for taxi game Rideshare Stimulator — although it denied replacing an actual human writer with the tech.

The question is, can voice actors actually do anything about it? In July last year, video game actors voted to end a year-long strike over AI protections, with about 2,500 members of U.S. union SAG-Aftra involved in the action against 10 of the biggest companies in the industry, including Activision and Electronic Arts. In a statement released after the vote to end the strike, the union said a new contract secured "consent and disclosure requirements for AI digital replica use."

That, however, doesn't prevent anyone from using the established AI platforms to create fake videos featuring well-known video game characters saying and doing pretty much anything they want.

Wesley is Director, News at IGN. Find him on Twitter at @wyp100. You can reach Wesley at wesley_yinpoole@ign.com or confidentially at wyp100@proton.me.

articles.title: Miskatonic Tales: Journey to Innsmouth Feels Less Like a Board Game and More Like a Tabletop RPG Without a GM
articles.summary: Miskatonic Tales: Journey to Innsmouth feels less like a board game and more like a fancy way to run a role-playing game without a GM.
articles.body:
If there’s one board game theme that rivals pleasing Renaissance-era nobles in popularity, it’s the works of H. P. Lovecraft. There’s just something about those tentacled horrors from outer space that seems to keep on appealing to tabletop adaptations. Just look at the ongoing acclaim heaped on Arkham Horror: The Card Game .

Miskatonic Tales: Journey to Innsmouth is the latest game to join this crowded lineage. But it’s attempting to stand out by taking a different route to the majority of its sticky, ichorous peers. A leaflet in the box suggests that you might want to go buy not another Lovecraftian board game but the role-playing game based on his works: Call of Cthulhu . This is more of a storytelling game than a strategy game.

The box is so hefty that you might worry it could actually contain an avatar of Nyarthatolep, but you can lift the lid in safety: the weight comes from the inclusion of three big spiral-bound books that contain the text paragraphs you’ll be referring to during the game. They’re good quality and will absolutely stand to be bent and flipped through time and time again. What’s less inspiring is the sheets of errata stickers you’ll need to paste onto various entries to ensure you have all the options the designers intended.

The remainder of the weight is mostly from several decks of cards. There are square location cards that are used to build the map, tarot-sized encounter cards for the bad guys you can meet on your adventures, and several standard playing-card sized decks. These include condition cards to track the bad – and occasionally beneficial – things that can happen to your character and a ton of skill cards that you’ll play to meet challenges. Most of these cards are purely informational, with solid graphic design that favors function over form but the location cards are graced with darkly evocative artwork.

It’s a similar story for the selection of character boards and their accompanying punch-out standees, representing an excellent variety of character types in every sense of the word, brought to life nicely in all their 1920s glory. There are lots of other, more workmanlike tokens to punch out, too, for tracking various actions and statuses during play.

Alongside the weighty components is an innocuous-looking, lightweight rulebook that you’ll quickly find is poorly laid out and worded. Everything you need to play is in there, but you’ll need repeated puzzled flip-throughs during setup and the first few turns before everyone is comfortable with what’s going on.

Broadly, your group will choose one of three missions, which are best played in order, and which you’ll work together to complete. You place a starting location and objective card and read an introductory paragraph of text which explains the various options that you have in that location. Most of them require you to discard one of your character’s skill cards to do something, while others require you to pass a skill check. This involves characters, often more than one if working together, to discard cards either of the skill type required for one automatic “success” towards the target number, or a card of a similar type to get a dice to roll which may, or may not, generate a success. You need enough successes to pass the target number in order to succeed.

In addition to the dice you get by generating cards you will also always roll a red dice in these checks. This can give you an extra success, but it can also roll scary-looking symbols like skulls or tentacles. These cause the matching track to increment and, often, to cause you to flip to a paragraph in the book, triggering an event in the in-game narrative, usually an undesirable one.

Running out of cards also causes a time track to increment with similar paragraphs along the route, putting you under a bit of pressure to hurry along and achieve your objectives. It’s a neat way of giving your adventures a sense of time and dynamism as you move through the locations.

You’ll spend a lot of your time in Miskatonic Tales reading paragraphs, not only from the tracks but when you enter a new location and in describing the results of your actions, pass or fail. You can appoint one person to read these out to the group, or take turns, or there’s a free app to download which will do it for you with very questionable voice acting. The writing is fine: it’s not overloaded with the obscure adjectives that Lovecraft was fond of, nor is it lifeless, but it’s not especially inspiring, either. It’s just about enough to set the scene and keep you engaged.

Where the paragraphs really shine is in giving you options. The choose your own adventure books this style of play derives from often leave players feeling as though they’d like to do things that aren’t offered as choices. That rarely happens here: there are paragraphs to interact in different ways with pretty much everything described. Indeed there are too many options to explore them all without running down your time track dangerously fast. You’ll need to pick and choose what you do based on your curiosity and your objectives.

The trouble is that you don’t have very much else beyond those two things to guide your picks. Again, like the gamebooks it evokes, most of the decision-making happens in the dark as you have very little information on which to guess which options are better than others. You can’t even really strategize around the skill check system beyond a bit of risk-reward analysis. The closest the game comes to giving you meaningful decisions are your use of when to spend magic points which give you re-rolls, and when to use each character’s special abilities. As a result, this feels less like a board game and more like a particularly fancy way to run a role-playing game without a GM.

You don’t even get much strategy or tactics when it comes to combat. Encounters can either be fought with weapons, if you have them, or via a different skill, either of which is resolved with the standard dice-rolling skill check mechanism. That’s pretty much the only choice you get. Damage is taken off your character’s health or sanity values and you can also take hits to these tracks from accumulating status cards like panic or injury that are given out by in-game events. If either track runs down to zero, that investigator is out of the game.

Win or lose, one thing the plethora of exploration options gives you is a decent amount of replay value. There’s a ton of stuff to do in Miksatonic Tales and a second attempt at a scenario can work out very differently from the first. The game has a neat keyword system that tracks how past decisions can impact future situations although, as per most of the game, you have no way of knowing how this will play out. Many of the choices lead to blind alleys or horrible punishments you cannot anticipate, which can feel frustrating but it suits the source material well enough. What it lacks in strategy, it makes up for in anticipation. However, whether you’ll want to replay a scenario is a moot point as game times run long, much of which is taken up by players reading out text. You can “save” your game to stretch it across multiple sessions if needs be.

articles.title: Curry, Wembanyama o Edwards, entre los 'reyes' del NBA 2K27: Estos son los líderes en cada estadística del juego
articles.standfirst: 2K publicaba el top 10 de jugadores en diferentes aparatados
articles.summary: 2K publicaba el top 10 de jugadores en diferentes aparatados
articles.body: La NBA acabó la temporada anterior, la 25/26 por todo lo alto con el anillo de los New York Knicks. Pero esta temporada que viene, la 26/27, no ha empezado de diferente manera, ya que hemos tenido un inicio espectacular, primero con el draft en el que tres nuevos españoles han llegado a la mejor liga de baloncesto del planeta, Aday Mara, Sergio de Larrea y Baba Miller, y más tarde con una agencia libre que nos ha dejado movimientos históricos que prometen cambiar la competición por completo. Giannis Antetokounmpo aterrizando en los Miami Heat era el primer gran movimiento que veíamos en la NBA de cara a la temporada que viene, el que pensábamos que, de lejos, sería el más impactante, pero no. Ya que el bombazo de Jalen Brown y LeBron James fichando por Philadelphia 76ers han dado un vuelco radical a una conferencia este más fuerte de lo que estábamos acostumbrados a ver. articles.title: Ni Hugo González ni Aday Mara, los españoles de la NBA se quedan fuera de 'las élites' del 2K27
articles.standfirst: Nuestros representantes en la mejor liga del mundo no están entre los mejores en el videojuego
articles.summary: Nuestros representantes en la mejor liga del mundo no están entre los mejores en el videojuego
articles.body: Como ocurre en cada inicio de la temporada de la NBA, el 2K, el mejor videojuego sobre la liga, también arranca una 'nueva vida' con el lanzamiento de una nueva edición. Y con este comienzo también tenemos mucha nueva información como por ejemplo los mejores jugadores del videojuego en cuanto a la valoración o los mejores jugadores en diferentes aspectos del juego como el tiro de tres, la defensa de perímetro o el manejo de balón, por ejemplo. Pues bien, de cara al NBA 2K27 tenemos malas noticias para nuestro país, por lo menos si hablamos de este videojuego, ya que ninguno de los españoles aparecen entre los mejores jugadores por valoración general, tanto en la lista global como la de los rookies, pero tampoco en los apartados de robos, tapones, defensa del perímetro, tiro de media distancia, tiro de tres, manejo de balón, velocidad con balón, salto vertical o mates, todas las categorías sobre las que tenemos rankings para 2K27. Y es que esta noticia pese a que sea negativa no nos pilla por sorpresa ya que ninguno tiene todavía esa consideración de estrella dentro de la liga. Pesa a esto podíamos pensar que por ejemplo Santi Aldama, un jugador bien considerado dentro de la NBA, podía estar entre los 100 mejores jugadores por media de la liga, y más viendo que los primeros en entrar en este top contaban solamente con un 81 de media. Pero además de este, si nos vamos a listas más específicas podíamos haber tenido representación como por ejemplo en la de los rookies, ya que Aday Mara, uno de los jugadores con más hype de este draft, elegido en el número 12, no se ha conseguido colar en el top 10 de novatos en 2K27. Y es que aunque quizá es soñar demasiado, el recién elegido por los Thunder podría haber tenido un hueco en el top 10 de taponadores por esa envergadura y capacidad para taponar tiros, aunque seguro que, aunque no esté ahora, lo veremos en un futuro. Para terminar nos vamos con Hugo González, el que ya en su primer año impresionó a toda la NBA por su capacidad de trabajo y defensa, por eso podíamos soñar con su presencia entre los 10 mejores de la liga en cuanto a robos, o mejor todavía, en defensa en el perímetro, la gran cualidad que ha mostrado el de los Celtics en su breve paso por la NBA, aunque, al igual que decíamos con Aday, si no está todavía en esta lista, estamos seguros de que lo veremos en el futuro.

articles.title: You can now just point at a mess and this robot vacuum will suck it up
articles.summary: A free update brings on-device gesture control and a Gemini-powered voice assistant to the WALL-E-style robot vacuum
articles.body: Matic, my current favorite robot vacuum, just got a big upgrade. The company has launched Matic Cues, which brings voice and gesture control to the robot. Now, you can talk directly to your vacuum to tell it what you want it to do, or just point at a mess to have it spot-clean.  The feature launches today, August 13 at 2 pm ET, and will show as an option in the Matic app under Settings > Matic Cues. The update arrives just ahead of a planned price hike on September 9, which will see the WALL-E-style robot’s price go from $1,245 to $1,495. I’ve been playing with Matic Cues for a day or so, and so far it’s working well. Gesture control is the standout feature here, as it’s something no other robot vacuum offers — the company’s founders are both computer vision engineers who worked at Google Nest cameras, and have been developing the feature since 2017.  [Video: Testing Matic Cues gesture control] It works by waking up the robot with the wake word “Hey, Matic,” then waiting for it to “see” me (by turning toward my voice). I then point to the mess, say “clean here,” and off it goes. I did notice that if I wanted it to target a smaller area, I needed to crouch down to point at it. If I gestured from standing height, it cleaned a wider area, taking longer. It can also follow me, so saying “Hey Matic, follow me,” walking to and pointing at the mess, started a clean-up.  Because it uses the robot’s existing vision hardware — which includes five cameras — gesture control works entirely on-device and is coming to all existing Matic robots. While most robot vacuums let you spot-clean by drawing a zone in the app, I’ve found that method to be imprecise and not useful for quick cleanups. Some can also respond to a “clean here” voice command, but that’s based on the general area where you’re standing; Matic’s gesture-based implementation feels more focused.  [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG_4180-copy.png?quality=90&strip=all] The new built-in voice assistant also worked smoothly in initial testing. Voice control isn’t new on robot vacuums — nearly all work with Alexa and Google and some with Apple’s Siri, and many now have their own onboard voice assistants — including Roborock, Ecovacs, and Narwal. I’ve had mixed success with these long-term. Most require remembering exact commands; while “vacuum the kitchen” is easy to remember, other phrases are less intuitive and less flexible than Matic’s offering.  Matic uses the Gemini API to understand natural language, including commands like “vacuum the inside of the carpet” (thus avoiding the tassels), “clean just the hard floors,” and “clean the toekicks in the kitchen” — something I always want done right after cooking dinner. [Image: The voice assistant can understand natural language; instead of telling it “Return to dock,” you can just tell it to ”Go away.“ https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG_8733.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] The robot could hear me from a room away and responded promptly — although it took a beat to go off and execute the command. It also doesn’t talk back; instead, its small display indicates it heard you and tells you what it’s doing. I was impressed how many commands it understood, including chained commands, like “clean the kitchen, vacuum the living room, and then mop the bathroom.” It also slunk back to its dock when I said, “Hey Matic, go away.” Handy if it’s underfoot when I’m cooking.  [Image: The voice assistant doesn’t talk back; it displays its confirmation of your command on its screen. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG_8731.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] One of Matic’s biggest selling points is that it doesn’t require the cloud and can be used without an internet connection. However, voice control does need both of those. While the company says the “Hey Matic” wake word is processed on-device, meaning no ambient chatter is sent to the cloud, any command after is sent to the Gemini API. A short chime tells you when anything is leaving the device. Mehul Nariyawala, cofounder and president of Matic, says the commands it sends are anonymized, adding that Matic chose cloud processing to support more than 75 languages and a wider variety of commands. The company plans to take the top 20 or 30 most-used commands and bring those locally in the future. Matic Cues is opt in, and you can turn it and the microphones off in settings. The trade-off between more convenience and more privacy is a constant tussle in the smart home. Roborock’s “Hey Rocky” voice assistant is entirely on device, but I rarely use it because it’s just not intuitive. So far I’ve found myself using “Hey Matic” much more frequently, as it’s just easier to talk to. The gesture control also solves a pain point I’ve long struggled with — getting a robot to clean the exact spot I want. For Matic users, this is a worthwhile update, and for those considering pulling the trigger, it’s a new convenience that makes a very good robot vacuum even better. Photos and video by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

articles.title: Satechi’s New Six-Port USB-C Desktop Charger Offers 240W of Power
articles.body:
Satechi has released the ChargeView 240W Desktop Charger , a compact desktop charging brick with six USB-C ports that outputs enough power to keep your favorite power-hungry handheld gaming PC , gaming laptop , smartphone , and more topped up all at once. It even has a screen for those who want to see just how much their gear is drawing.

That 240W is a measure of the device’s total output, not any one USB-C outlet, but Satechi’s new charger can still push out 140W from either of its first two front-facing ports. That’ll charge a 16-inch MacBook Pro at full speed and is more than enough to max out the capacity of any handheld gaming PC you throw at it. The 240W Desktop Charger can also offer up to 100W on its second two ports, and up to 30W on the last two. Altogether, it has more ports and faster charging than most of IGN's current favorite USB-C chargers, both in general and for specific devices like the Steam Deck .

Satechi says its display can show the real-time power draw from each port, and that the charger “auto-detects each device’s requirements and balances output across active ports, keeping everything charged efficiently, quietly, and without overheating.” The product comes with a stand that lets you both rest the Desktop Charger horizontally or vertically, with a slight tilt so it’s easier to see the display. The charger comes in one color, Space Black.

The ChargeView 240W Desktop Charger costs $150 and is available now at Satechi’s website and Amazon .

Wes is a freelance writer (Freelance Wes, they call him) who has covered technology, gaming, and entertainment steadily since 2020 at Gizmodo, Tom's Hardware, Hardcore Gamer, and most recently, The Verge. Inside of him there are two wolves: one that thinks it wouldn't be so bad to start collecting game consoles again, and the other who also thinks this, but more strongly.

articles.title: Lanterns Series Premiere Review: How HBO’s True Detective-Style Superhero Mystery Reinvigorates James Gunn's DCU
articles.summary: With a finely honed Dynamic Duo lighting the way, Lanterns serves as a critical return to form for the DCU in its first episode. Read our spoiler-free review.

This is a spoiler-free review of the first episode of Lanterns Season 1. The series debuts on HBO and HBO Max on Sunday, August 16.

It’s safe to say that a lot is riding on the first season of Lanterns . This is one of the first key pieces of James Gunn and Peter Safran’s DCU that isn’t directly steered by Gunn himself. We’ve seen enough by now to know that Gunn himself has a solid handle on the DC brand. Creature Commandos, Superman, and Peacemaker have all been enjoyable. But can this fledgling cinematic universe thrive when he hands the reins over to other creators? Supergirl certainly calls that into question , casting doubt on Gunn’s lofty claims about strong scripts and clear artistic visions being the driving force of this line. The DCU needs a win right about now, and I’m happy to say that Lanterns is ready and able to deliver in its first episode.

Granted, it’s been tough to know what exactly to make of this series. For a franchise as fundamentally fantastical as this one, the prospect of focusing on an Earth-based murder mystery and downplaying the actual Green Lantern elements wasn’t necessarily appealing to all fans. The initial Lanterns trailer did little to assuage the fears of those concerned by that premise. And then co-creator Damon Lindelof really stepped in it with some of his comments, to the point where no less a DC authority than Grant Morrison felt compelled to clap back . Suffice it to say, DC and Warners didn’t really do themselves any favors with the marketing of Lanterns, but the proof is ultimately in the pudding.

Yes, Lanterns is essentially what the trailers and early previews have made it out to be. It’s as much a True Detective and Slow Horses-style murder mystery as it is a superhero drama (and, in fact, features veterans of both shows among its creative team). It’s not necessarily going to appeal to viewers intent on seeing the cosmic side of the Green Lantern mythos on full display. We rarely even see Kyle Chandler’s Hal Jordan put on the costume. And given how ugly and clunky this live-action rendition of the suit really is, that’s probably a good thing. The series generally looks good, but more in that quietly stylized, more grounded True Detective way than because of any budget-busting special effects. In short, Green Lantern purists who want unadulterated, comic book-accurate, ring-slinging cosmic spectacle are setting themselves up for disappointment with this show.

But for those willing to abandon preconceived notions and take Lanterns for what it is, this strange combination of superhero adventure and terrestrial murder mystery works surprisingly well. A lot of that comes down to the chemistry between Chandler’s Hal and his trainee, Aaron Pierre’s John Stewart. Hal has never been portrayed as the nicest or most well-adjusted member of the Justice League in various DC media, but here he’s downright hostile and standoffish to his young charge. As much as the first episode lays the foundation for an urgent investigation in the remote town of Rushville, Nebraska, it makes it clear that the real conflict is between Hal and John. One is a cocky, grizzled veteran suspicious that his space cop handlers are trying to replace him. The other is a former Marine with a deep desire for the ring but limited tolerance for shenanigans. To say the two butt heads in the first episode is putting it mildly indeed.

The series leans a lot on that core dynamic, making it crucial that it finds the right actors for the job. That’s one area where Lanterns succeeds unequivocally. Both actors are pitch-perfect in their portrayals of these iconic (if sometimes barely recognizable) characters. Chandler probably isn’t the first name to pop up on anyone’s list of dream Hal Jordan actors. He wasn’t even DC’s original choice for the part , it seems. And were the series striving for a more traditional, youthful take on the character, Chandler would obviously be a poor fit. But that’s not the goal here. This is a version of Hal who’s been active in the DCU for decades and truly feels the weight of those years. Chandler expertly captures that unique blend of exasperation, paranoia, and deep-seated overconfidence that define the DCU’s Hal Jordan. The last thing he feels like doing is training the guy who’s trying to steal his job, and he makes that clear in every interaction with John.

As for John, Pierre brings a quiet, no-nonsense charisma to the screen that contrasts nicely with Hal’s fiery bravado. John is quiet, composed, and stoic, qualities that could make for a very boring role in the wrong hands. Fortunately, Pierre is able to bring enough subtle nuance to the screen that his character never comes across as dull or underdeveloped. He’s reserved, but underneath it all he burns with desire. We see how badly he wants the ring, even if it means putting up with an endless stream of nonsense from his superior officer.

It’s also nice to see the first episode dig a little bit into the racial undertones of this Training Day-esque dynamic. In one scene, a seething John calls his father for advice and is reminded that white men like Hal Jordan have the privilege of being eccentric and difficult. Not so for a Black man trying to prove his worthiness for the most exclusive law enforcement gig in the entire universe. At least at this early stage, it doesn’t appear that Lanterns is going to be steeped in the racial tensions of modern America to the same degree that Lindelof’s previous DC series was , but it’s still satisfying to have that element acknowledged – especially given how important John Stewart was to the early diversification of DC’s comic book universe decades ago.

On the subject of John Stewart, Sr. (played as a young man by J. Alphonse Nicholson and an older man by Sherman Augustus), the premiere teases a very intriguing dynamic there that’s sure to be explored in future episodes. It’s such a common trope for superhero media to paint their protagonists as orphans yearning for a lost father figure. That’s even baked into Hal’s origin story. But Lanterns is clearly striving for something much different with John’s family background, adding in new layers and details that aren’t necessarily taken from the comics. It’s a useful reminder that while the series isn’t afraid to alter the source material in sometimes profound ways, those alterations are about more than simply making Green Lantern practical in a small-screen format.

Once the Hal/John dynamic is firmly established, the premiere sets about laying the groundwork for the murder mystery that looks to be fueling the conflict in Season 1. To be frank, said mystery isn’t the reason to tune into the series, at least at this early stage. It gets the job done in terms of moving the plot from A to B, but for now the conflict is pretty small in scope. It’s mostly about Hal’s uphill battle to convince everyone around him (John included) that the dead bodies in front of them have extraterrestrial ties.

Here again, the various characters and their interpersonal clashes are what make the series shine. Early in the episode, viewers are introduced to another major character in Kelly Macdonald’s Kerry, the no-nonsense sheriff in charge of keeping the peace in the formerly quiet town of Rushville. As much as Chandler and Pierre’s icy dynamic fuels the series in its first episode, there’s also plenty of fun to be had in the equally standoffish relationship between Hal and Sheriff Kerry. There’s all the bickering over jurisdiction and one-sided flirtation you’d expect. Kerry quickly develops into a very fun, likable character who’s every bit the effective foil to Hal that John is.

Rounding out the notable cast members introduced in Episode 1 are Garret Dillahunt as local cowboy/ranch tycoon William Macon and Poorna Jagannathan as another Rushville native named Zoe. Macon serves his purpose as a charming but quietly unsettling antagonist figure with murky ties to the town’s murder mystery. Zoe, meanwhile, quickly strikes up a close bond with John, allowing the series to explore shades of the character that aren’t possible through Hal alone. Rushville is a small town full of interesting personalities, offering plenty of room for growth in the coming seven episodes.

Again, the murder mystery itself gets the job done in terms of plot catalysts, but it’s the characters who tend to shine more than the plot in Episode 1. It is worth noting, however, that the premiere keeps one big reveal under its hat until the final moments. This twist is sure to be as controversial as anything the show has to offer in its debut chapter. But as far as throwing viewers off-guard and hinting at a larger, more ambitious scope for the series, it delivers just what’s needed. If the prospect of plainclothes Green Lanterns loudly squabbling and rubbing elbows with cowboys isn’t enough to lure you in, this twist might just do the trick.

articles.title: A Senate subcommittee has opened an investigation into Roblox over child safety.
articles.summary:
“Roblox appears to prioritize revenue and engagement metrics over the safety and well-being of our children, and the alleged criminal activity on Roblox warrants congressional scrutiny,” Senators Josh Hawley (R-MO) and Dick Durbin (D-IL) wrote in a letter to Roblox CEO David Baszucki.
The online gaming platform has also been subject to state lawsuits regarding alleged child safety issues. Roblox has settled some of those lawsuits, and it recently launched dedicated accounts for younger users.
[Link: Hawley, Durbin Launch Investigation into Child Sexual Abuse on Roblox | https://www.hawley.senate.gov/hawley-durbin-launch-investigation-into-child-sexual-abuse-on-roblox/ | Josh Hawley, U.S. Senator for Missouri]

articles.title: Wembanyama se 'cuela' en el olimpo de NBA 2K27: Estos son los 10 mejores jugadores del videojuego
articles.standfirst: El juego de baloncesto publicaba las mejores valoraciones de la próxima edición
articles.summary: El juego de baloncesto publicaba las mejores valoraciones de la próxima edición
articles.body: El próximo 4 de septiembre NBA 2K27 llegará a nuestras vidas de manera completa, ya que, aunque hasta ese día no podamos tener en nuestras consolas el juego final, ya ha ido entrando en nuestro día a día poco a poco, sobre todo con toda la información que ha salido sobre el próximo título de baloncesto durante estas últimas semanas. Hablamos, por ejemplo, de las medias de los mejores jugadores. Y es que además de que se han publicado los tops 10 de ciertas estadísticas como el tiro de tres, tapones o defensa del perímetro, también se han hecho oficiales las medias de los 100 mejores jugadores del NBA 2K27, un proceso que siempre genera mucha expectación y que ayer finalizaba con la publicación del top 10, un ranking en el que más que sorpresas, vemos la consagración de una estrella de la liga que puede convertirse en leyenda. Hablamos, como no podía ser de otra manera, de Victor Wembanyama, la estrella de los Spurs que tras su año de consagración en la liga siendo totalmente dominante y rozando el anillo en esa final contra los Knicks con solo 22 años, se ha conseguido colar entre el olimpo del NBA 2K27. Con esto nos referimos a que mientras antes eran Shai y Jokic los dos jugadores con más media, este año el francés se ha unido a este dúo con 97 de media para formar un 'trono a tres'. Pero a las puertas de este podio se ha quedado otro jugador que el año pasado elevó mucho su estatus dentro de la liga. Este es Jalen Brunson, el campeón de la NBA y MVP de las finales, el que con una subida hasta el 96 de media empata con Luka Doncic y Giannis Antetokounmpo en ese segundo escalón del NBA 2K27. Ya para cerrar el top 10 del NBA 2K27 ha colocado a Anthony Edwards (95) y Cade Cunningham (94) en séptima y octava posición y para cerrar a dos auténticas leyendas del baloncesto que se mantienen entre los diez mejores jugadores del videojuego pese a que ya están más cerca de los 40 que de los 30. Hablamos de Curry y Kevin Durant, los que cierran el top con un 93 de valoración.

articles.title: Estos son los 100 mejores jugadores de NBA 2K27: LeBron y Curry se mantienen en el top
articles.standfirst: 2K publicaba las valoraciones de los mejores jugadores de la NBA
articles.summary: 2K publicaba las valoraciones de los mejores jugadores de la NBA
articles.body: Una nueva temporada de la NBA está a la vuelta de la esquina, lo que también significa, por supuesto, una nueva edición del NBA 2K, en este caso el NBA 2K27, el que llega a nuestras consolas el próximo 4 de septiembre y que, como nuevo, va desvelando diferentes detalles cuanto más próximo esté este día. Y una de las cosas que siempre generan más expectación son las valoraciones de los jugadores, especialmente el top 100. Pues bien, además de esto también hemos podido ver los líderes de las diferentes estadísticas o apartados del juegos más específicos como por ejemplo el de tapones (Wembanyama), robos (Ausar Thompson), tiro de media distancia (Shai Gilgeous-Alexander), defensa del perímetro (Ausar Thompson), manejo de balón (Kyrie Irving), velocidad con el balón (De'Aaron Fox), mates (Anthony Edwards), salto vertical (Amen Thompson) o tiro de tres (Stephen Curry). Además, para desgracia de los aficionados españoles a la NBA y amantes del videojuego de nuestro país no vamos a tener representación en ninguno de estos rankings de estadísticas y tampoco en el top 100 de mejores jugadores, ya que Santi Aldama, nuestro jugador con más caché dentro de la NBA, no ha subido tanto de media por su desempeño en la pasada temporada como para colarse en esta prestigiosa lista. Como decíamos antes lo más interesante es el top 100 de valoraciones del NBA 2k27, ya que, de alguna manera, sirve para ver quiénes son los mejores jugadores de toda la NBA. Y como es normal, en este tipo de ranking siempre hay sorpresas. Un ejemplo es la media de Dylan Harper (85) y Kon Knueppel (84), ya que el primero cuenta con más media que el segundo. Y es que aunque el de los Spurs llegara a las finales en su año de novato, el de los Hornets firmó una temporada histórica, solo superada por Cooper Flagg, el que en 2K27 contará con una media de 87.

articles.title: Drakong’s New Attack on Titan-Themed Collectible Controllers Come in a Blind Box
articles.summary: These cute, keychain-sized controllers look a bit like a pixelated NES controller paired with one of several characters from Attack on Titan, and will be available via a somewhat unconventional manner: a blind box.
articles.body:
Drakong, a sub-brand of Hyperkin, today announced the PixelByte controller range , a new line of collectible controllers themed after Attack on Titan. These cute, keychain-sized controllers look a bit like a pixelated NES controller paired with one of several characters from Attack on Titan, and will be available via a somewhat unconventional manner: a blind box.

Despite their size, layout, and distribution method, the PixelByte controllers are fully functional, compatible with PC, Switch 1 and 2, iOS, Android, and other Bluetooth devices. They offer approximately 12 hours of wireless gameplay, and are rechargeable via USB-C.

Each PixelByte blind box contains one of seven possible variants, pairing a unique colorway with a chibi charm of Attack on Titan characters like Eren, Mikasa, Levi, and Hange. There's also one rare chase variant that's found at a lower rate than the rest.

I can't say that a blind box is the most idea way to buy a controller, so I doubt the PixelByte line will make our list of the best controllers for PC or Switch , but I could see the appeal from the collectible side of things. I'm personally not one for blind boxes, but my Pokémon card collection will attest that I'm very familiar with the concept of cracking open physical loot boxes at the prospect of scoring something rare and shiny.

The PixelByte controllers are available for pre-order now for $24.99 per box.

Bo Moore is IGN's Senior Manager of Tech. You can find him online @usebomswisely.

articles.title: Ikea is teasing a collaboration with Xbox.
articles.summary:
The Swedish flatpack furniture maker shared a video through its Instagram account today that seemingly reveals an upcoming collection inspired by the console. articles.title: Brandon Sanderson's Cosmere RPG Starter Set Is Now Being Sold at Target Retail Stores
articles.body:
The Cosmere RPG was first released last year, but it only recently hit a major milestone for tabletop games: It's available at Target. If you're looking for a copy of the Stormlight Starter set, you can currently pick it up at your local Target store for only $24.99.

"It's hard to get our things into these non-traditionally book sales markets, so we're really excited that Target was willing to give us a try," said Brandon Sanderson in his most recent YouTube update . "So, you can grab this and you can start into the RPG and Target will think that we're cool and maybe they will carry other Brandon Sanderson stuff in the future."

Target has long been a place to buy board games, but it is fairly rare to see a traditional tabletop RPG on the shelves. The addition of something like Brandon Sanderson's Cosmere RPG at a store like Target is good news for other book-to-tabletop adaptations looking to break through. It may seem like a fairly niche market, but we've already seen big success for the Dungeon Crawler Carl RPG earlier this year so it's clear there's a growing interest for these sorts of things.

Sanderson also pointed out that the starter set includes the Bridge Nine adventure, which is meant to introduce players to RPG mechanics. He also said that there "aren't any book spoilers in the starter set", so you don't need to worry about ruining someone's Cosmere book journey if they haven't started the Stormlight Archive just yet.

Sanderson has worked with Brotherwise Games on a number of other tabletop adaptations and doesn't appear to be slowing down anytime soon. The next big game is set to be Stormlight: War for Roshar , which is set to hit Kickstarter in the fall of 2026 .

Outside of the tabletop space, Sanderson has recently stated that he's finished the first draft of his Mistborn screenplay . The first Cosmere movie adaptation will eventually be coming to Apple TV, but there has yet to be any sort of release date attached.

Jacob Kienlen is a Senior Audience Development Strategist and Writer for IGN. Born and raised in Portland, Oregon, he has considered the Northwest his home for his entire life. With a bachelor's degree in communication and 10 years of professional writing experience, his expertise is spread across a variety of different pop culture topics -- from TV series to books and the latest LEGO sets..

articles.title: Ni los Knicks ni los Spurs, el 'All-Star' de Philadelphia 76ers amenaza la NBA y el 2K27
articles.standfirst: LeBron James, Embiid, Jalen Brow, Maxey y Edgecombe forman un quintento temible en la realidad y en el videojuego
articles.summary: LeBron James, Embiid, Jalen Brow, Maxey y Edgecombe forman un quintento temible en la realidad y en el videojuego
articles.body: El NBA 2K27 ya está a la vuelta de la esquina, tanto es así que el próximo 4 de septiembre será cuando podamos probar el videojuego final. Pues bien, pese a que aún no tengamos en nuestras manos el título de baloncesto, estamos teniendo mucho contenido previo que está dando de que hablar. Hablamos, por ejemplo, de las medias oficiales de los jugadores, más en concreto de las de los 100 jugadores mejor valorados en 2K27, las que se han ido haciendo oficiales con el paso de los días. Esto es siempre algo muy interesante, pues sirve en muchas ocasiones como orientación para ver el estatus de cada jugador dentro de la liga ya que el juego es un reflejo de lo que ocurre sobre el parqué. Pues bien, con estás valoraciones nos encontramos algunas curiosidades como el All-Star que han conseguido montar los Philadelphia 76ers. Y es que durante estas semanas marcadas por los fichajes en la NBA el gran protagonista ha sido el equipo de la conferencia este, ya que al núcleo formado por Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey y V. J. Edgecombe han conseguido sumarle a dos estrellas del nivel de Jalen Brown y LeBron James, montando así un quinteto temible que ya piensa en anillo. Y este superequipo no solo mete miedo en la NBA real, ya que en el NBA 2K27 parece irreal. Decimos esto porque las valoraciones que han conseguido juntar los 76ers parece de un equipo del All-Star, siendo el eslabón más débil V. J. Edgecombe con una media de 83 estando igualmente entre los 80 juegdores con mejor valoración. Pero lo increíble llega en las otras cuatro posiciones, ya que todos están dentro del top 20 de mejores jugadores del NBA 2K27. Y curiosamente, de las cuatro estrellas la que mejor valorada está es Tyrese Maxey con una media de 92, mientras Jalen Brown, Joel Embiid y LeBron James empezarán en el videojuego con una valoración de 91, formando así un quinteto que es igual de temible en la vida real y en el videojuego.

articles.title: NBA 2K27 presenta todas sus novedades: Desde una Ciudad mixta a una carrera en la era de Jordan
articles.standfirst: El videojuego hacía la presentación de todo lo que tendremos a partir del 4 de septiembre
articles.summary: El videojuego hacía la presentación de todo lo que tendremos a partir del 4 de septiembre
articles.body: El NBA 2K27 ya está a punto de llegar a nuestras casas, ya que el próximo 4 de septiembre será cuando se lance de manera oficial en todo el mundo. Y como es normal, a tan poco tiempo del lanzamiento mucha ha sido la información que se ha ido revelando con el paso de los días. Hablamos por ejemplo de los tops de estadísticas, es decir, los 10 mejores jugadores en el tiro de tres, en tapones, en mates o en manejo de balón, pero también las valoraciones de los mejores jugadores del juego, más concretamente de los 100 con mejor media. Pues bien, esto se ha quedado en nada con lo que vivimos ayer, ya que 2K revelaba mucha información sobre el videojuego, la que te contamos aquí abajo. Y es que este año 2K quiere que el juego sea lo más equilibrado posible, metiendo mejoras en ataque pero también en defensa, todas ellas al servicio de ProPLAY, una herramienta con la que tendremos mayor realismo por unas animaciones más fieles a la realidad. En NBA 2K27 tendremos una gran variedad de animaciones, tanto es así que se nos promete que ninguna entrada a canasta por ejemplo será igual que la siguiente. Pero quizá lo que más ha llamado la atención de todos son dos aspectos. El primero el medidor de mates, el que tendremos que coordinar cada vez que queramos machar el aro, pero en esta ocasión mejorado respecto a NBA 2K26, más natural e intuitivo. Esto en cuanto al ataque, pero en cuanto a la defensa quizá lo más importante es el nuevo sistema de punteo, es decir, que parece que en este juego sí valdrá intentar puntear los tiros del rival sin hacer falta y que supondrá un obstáculo real para el adversario. Pero entrando ya a los modos de juego empezamos con MyNBA, esta modalidad en la que tomas las riendas de un equipo de la NBA y manejas todo a tu antojo, es decir, el general manager, el entrenador, la agencia libre, las renovaciones... Y es que aquí más que grandes innovaciones, 2K ha decidido mejorar lo que ya tenía con diferentes puntos claves como por ejemplo haciendo unas negociaciones contractuales más realistas y un sistema de confianza del general manager totalmente nuevo. Pero aunque no haya grandes innovaciones en lo que ya teníamos, sí que hay una gran novedad, algo gigante e ilusionante. Y es que ahora tendremos MyNBA Legacy, un universo de 100 años en el que podremos elegir a nuestro jugador favorito y devolverlo a su estado de novato, subirlo de nivel y forjar una trayectoria profesional sin precedentes, algo con lo que podremos modificar la historia del baloncesto. Pero seguramente una de las novedades más interesantes e importantes de este NBA 2K27 es que tendremos la primera Ciudad mixta de la historia del videojuego, así que podremos subir a nuestro personaje de nivel y 'chulear' por las canchas de la Ciudad independientemente de si tenemos a un hombre o una mujer. Algo importante, para que todos los jugadores cuentan con las mismas herramientas, los personajes masculinos y femeninos contarán con la misma estructura, altura, insignias, atributos y envergadura, así solo importarán las builds de cada uno y las manos con las que juguemos. Además de esto como ocurre cada año la Ciudad contará con una renovación estética, tanto de ropa, pues se implementarán también atuendos femeninos, como de escenarios, ya que tendremos más pistas al aire libre y nuevas apariencias de las pistas de REC por ejemplo. Y es que este año contamos con tres grandes novedades en el apartado de 'Mi Carrera'. El primero de ellos es que podremos tener nuestra carrera en diferentes momentos de la historia del baloncesto, es decir, que podemos empezar a jugar en la época actual o en la era de Kobe, de Magic vs. Bird o de Jordan entre otras, las que contarán con momentos específicos que ocurrieron por aquel entonces. Pero si eliges la era actual viene la segunda novedad y es que estarás inmerso en "Fuego y Hormigón", la historia de MyCareer de NBA 2K27, la más larga hasta la fecha en NBA 2K con 11 capítulos en la que empezaremos como un universitario en Duke y terminaremos, si no la liamos mucho, siendo una estrella de la NBA. Pero esto no es todo, ya que la tercera novedad no se queda atrás. Y es que en la carrera de NBA 2K27 podremos jugar con una amigo en modo cooperativo, es decir, que podrá manejar de manera simultánea a Trace Miller, un personaje de la historia que conocemos en la G League y que llegará con nosotros a la NBA que nos permitirá pasar grandes momentos con nuestro amigo en un modo que siempre ha sido muy solitario. Tanto la carrera como la ciudad giran en torno a una cosa, MyPlayer, y es que la creación de nuestro personaje es fundamental en NBA 2K. Por eso tenemos buenas noticias, ya que 2K promete el creador de nuestro jugador más versátil de la historia para que podamos parecernos lo máximo posible a nuestra estrella favorita de la liga. Y es que además de tener más insignias, mayor progresión y un mayor número de animaciones, es decir, que nos tendremos que explotar todavía más la cabeza para crear a nuestro jugador, como decíamos antes nos podremos crear por primera vez en la historia personajes femeninos de la misma manera que los masculinos. Pero la gran novedad es que el 21 de agosto se pondrá en funcionamiento NBA 2K HQ, una aplicación con la que podremos estar pendientes de NBA 2K27 las 24 horas del día y cuya función principal será crear a nuestro jugador ya que te da acceso al creador de MyPLAYER completo de NBA 2K27 para que puedas crear a tu jugador desde donde quieras para utilizarlo en tu consola. Como decíamos al principio de la noticia NBA 2K27 saldrá de manera definitiva el 4 de septiembre, pero estaba previsto un acceso anticipado si contabas con la Edición Deluxe o superior el 28 de agosto. Pues bien, ayer en esta presentación la mayor sorpresa de todas era que este acceso anticipado se adelantaba dos días. Es decir que si tienes reservada la edición Deluxe o Superior podrás jugar al NBA 2K27 el próximo 26 de agosto, por lo que, sumado a la apertura de NBA 2K HQ del 21 de agosto, podremos bucear por el videojuego mucho antes de lo que pensábamos.

articles.title: Don't Skip Your Chance to Compete in The UNO Championship Series, With a $50,000 Grand Finale Prize
articles.summary: How good are you at UNO? Toy company Mattel is announcing the UNO World Championship Series, which will offer a $50,000 grand prize.
articles.body:
How good are you at UNO? This year, toy company Mattel is announcing the UNO World Championship Series, which will take the fast-paced card game to the world stage with a $50,000 grand prize.

Fancy your chances? Taking a shot at the tournament is as easy as joining in via the UNO! Mobile app, or turning up to in-person qualifiers to be held across the country in Orlando (October 3), Chicago (October 10) and Los Angeles (October 17).

Successful contestants will then compete on the world stage in the UNO World Championship grand final, broadcast live from L.A. on November 11, and available to watch globally via Twitch.

If the honor of being crowed the UNO World Champion isn't enough of a draw (pun intended), then the $50,000 prize money will likely sweeten the deal (sorry).

"At its core, UNO has always been about creating unforgettable moments around the table from epic comebacks to game-changing Draw 4s," Katie Buford, VP and Global Head of Mattel Games said. "The 2026 UNO Championship Series Tournament brings that excitement to the biggest stage yet, giving fans around the world a front-row seat as elite players battle it out to become this year's UNO champion."

Can't make it to L.A.? No worries. If you want to up your UNO game to the championship level then Mattel is launching a range of prize-worthy products for you to play with at home. These include the UNO Championship Series Tournament Set ($19.99) which includes a snazzy UNO set, scoring pad and gold trophy.

A separate UNO Championship Series Belt ($19.99) will also be available, as will a Championship Series Card Shuffler ($19.99). For the pros, the UNO Championship Series Expanded Tournament Set ($27.99) is the ultimate offering, with a more robust gold trophy for the champ.

Tom Phillips is IGN's News Editor. You can reach Tom at tom_phillips@ign.com or find him on Bluesky @tomphillipseg.bsky.social

articles.title: The Pixel 11 Pro is a great phone, no thanks to its flashiest new features
articles.summary: Forget HiLight and Proactive Assistance. The Pixel 11 Pro is at its best with focused new tools that actually work.
articles.body: Google is trying to get you off your phone. The Pixel 11 Pro is “A Phone Designed to Help You Use It Less,” the company promises. It can proactively help you book restaurant reservations, take the best frames from a video, and help you voice-text significantly faster. The pitch is that the new features bundled with the Pixel 11 series of phones can help fix your relationship with technology — one that Google knows has badly degraded in recent years. But the hardware of the Pixel 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL is very similar to last year’s models — and in at least one case, a downgrade — so those software features are pretty much the entire pitch.  Over the last week testing the 11 Pro, I’ve been trying them all to see how much they can help me put my phone down. Like many experiences with Google software, when they work, they are genuinely helpful. But getting them to work often requires a very narrow set of circumstances that some Google engineer probably dreamed up in the “society if” utopia lab. Google wants you to be living your life, with your phone placed face down on the table so it can’t distract you unless HiLight notifies you of something you need to pay attention to. When I use Gemini, I’m generally typing to it, and when I do use Gemini voice mode, my phone is in my hand or sitting screen up. If this was just one of the many things HiLight could light up for, I wouldn’t find it so offensive. But at the moment, the only other thing HiLight will glow for is for calls from your favorite contacts. I wish I was kidding. [Image: The only options for HiLight. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/HiLight-Example-Pixel-11-Pro.png?quality=90&strip=all] If I’m getting a call from a favorite contact, I just want my phone to ring. Again, if it was just an additional feature, then sure, I guess. I don’t mind having an additional indicator that a favorite is calling me while my phone is face down. It is a genuinely great feature, saves me time, and almost makes it feel like I’m having a conversation in real time while texting. The feature is front and center in the camera app right next to the photo and video modes, which tells you something about how confident Google is in it. Start a Magic Capture, point it at what’s happening, and when you’re done recording, Gemini will do some processing and pull out what it considers the best photos and video clips from the session. During the Made by Google keynote last week, Google demoed the feature by recording some people shooting hoops on a basketball court. In the demonstration, Google said you could simply hold your phone and let it record while you take in the moment with your eyes. I have tried this exact scenario quite a few times, and let me tell you, it is extremely difficult to keep your subject in frame if you’re not staring at your screen. Magic Capture did a great job of pulling relevant images and clips from my recordings when I was making sure to keep my subject in frame by, you know, staring at my screen, but unless you have your phone mounted on a tripod or something, it’s naive to think you can ignore your phone completely. That caveat aside, I really like this feature. I take a lot of videos on my phone, but I’m much more likely to revisit pictures. With Magic Capture, I can have both. The main caveat seems to be that stabilization isn’t as good on the clips it cuts compared to clips you’d take in video mode. Even so, I think Magic Capture will be useful for parents trying to capture moments of their kids, without needing to work so hard to get the perfect smile for a photo. Instead of marketing this feature as something that lets you be in the moment by not looking at your phone at all, it would probably be better to pitch it as something that will automatically grab great photos and short video clips for you, and all you need to do is point your phone and hit record. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Camera-Sample-Shadows-120x-zoom.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] While Magic Capture took most of the spotlight in Google’s keynote, maybe the most discussed photo upgrade this year is Camera Looks. I did a whole interview with Google’s camera chief about this feature going deep into how the new system was made, and there’s a lot of potential in the execution. Camera Looks is a new photography feature you can think of similar to Fujifilm’s film simulations, which let its cameras emulate different film styles on the JPGs they put out. On the Pixel 11 series, there are four modifications of the standard camera, with Original, Natural, Shadows, and Vanilla giving subtle tweaks to your image. But if you want to get more out there, there are six additional creative looks, called Editorial, Velvet, Classic, Digi, Black Tie, and Minimal. Each of the looks can be modified to your liking, with adjustable settings like contrast, highlights, shadows, vibrance, tint, warmth, sharpness, and grain. What makes this a really interesting feature to me is that Google is adjusting the amount of computational processing it’s doing at capture, based on the settings you choose; it’s not just applying filters later. For example, the Digi mode will do less frame stacking and the Minimal mode will apply less sharpness and contrast. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Camera-Looks-Sample.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Camera-Looks-Sample-9.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Camera-Looks-Sample-8.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Camera-Looks-Sample-7.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Camera-Looks-Sample-6.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Camera-Looks-Sample-5.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Camera-Looks-Sample-4.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Camera-Looks-Sample-3.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Pixel-11-Pro-Black-Tie-Camera-Look.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] I really dig the looks, even right out of the box. They span from basic edits to quite inspired, and if you’re looking for something that gives you the “film simulation look” straight out of camera, these definitely deliver. It was high time Google added some more creative looks to the Pixel, especially considering it doesn’t have nearly as robust a third-party camera ecosystem as the iPhone. I’ve personally made the Minimal mode permanent on my phone for its unsharpened, minimally contrasty look, occasionally switching to Classic, but after testing them all, I think Velvet and Editorial will get a lot of use, since they have the most “film aesthetic” of the bunch. With less processed photos, you can actually see texture in photos, which is normally washed away by noise reduction algorithms. Overall camera quality on the Pixel 11 Pro series is great this year, and practically the only reason to pick up a Pro Pixel over the standard 11, aside from wanting a larger phone, in the case of the XL. The primary sensor is technically new, but Google tells me it’s the same size as last year and was swapped in because it uses slightly less power. The biggest camera hardware change is the new larger telephoto sensor, which Google says captures more light, and I can tell. Telephoto cameras are usually the weakest link in a smartphone’s camera arsenal, but even at 10x zoom, which is a 2x crop of the telephoto sensor, it was hard to notice any significant quality degradation. Plus, the transition between sensors is much smoother now, with only a very slight jump when switching between lenses. [Image: The Camera Looks interface. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Google-Pixel-11-Pro-Taking-Photo-Camera-Looks-Velvet.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The Pixel 11 Pro also includes a 120x Pro Zoom mode, enabled by the new image signal processor in Tensor G6. Like the 100x Pro Zoom on the Pixel 10 Pro, Google is using generative AI to upscale your highly zoomed-in images to make them look more realistic. On objects without a lot of sharp edges this actually does a pretty good job, and Google will give you both the non-AI-enhanced and enhanced versions so you can see the difference. I was in Spain during last week’s solar eclipse, and the Pixel 11 Pro did a good job of turning a zoomed-in photo of the moon from a blurry mess into something that looked good enough to elicit responses of awe when I posted it in Slack. But that was a relatively simple image, and shots with a lot more detail often look like an early AI-generated image, with skewed angles and edges, garbled text, and muddy tones. I’d only really use this if you needed to see information you can’t see with your normal eyes, not for artistic purposes. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Pixel-11-Pro-Super-Res-Zoom-100x.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Pixel-11-Pro-Super-Res-Zoom-120x.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The Pixel 11 Pro also gets a new, faster Night Sight, which Google says is about three times faster on average than the Pixel 10 Pro. In testing, most Night Sight images I took only needed to be held for one second, and I got all the same benefits you got from holding the phone for three or more seconds previously. This is the kind of quality-of-life update I love to see, and I’m glad Google is continuing to improve here. I love Rambler, Magic Capture, and Camera Looks. If you’re looking to upgrade your phone this year, they’re legitimately great features. But after a week of use, it’s clear to me that the Pixel 11 Pro is not yet smart enough to help me use my phone less, despite what Google claims. Proactive Assistance is only bound to save you a few seconds and a few taps compared to just opening the apps and doing the steps yourself. If you were hoping for the Pixel 11 Pro would help address your phone addiction, that’s probably not going to happen. But if you’re looking for a phone with the best voice-to-text on the market, great cameras with good built-in style, and solid hardware, the Pixel 11 Pro delivers.  Photography by David Imel / The Verge

Magic Capture did a great job of pulling relevant images and clips from my recordings when I was making sure to keep my subject in frame by, you know, staring at my screen, but unless you have your phone mounted on a tripod or something, it’s naive to think you can ignore your phone completely. That caveat aside, I really like this feature. I take a lot of videos on my phone, but I’m much more likely to revisit pictures. With Magic Capture, I can have both. The main caveat seems to be that stabilization isn’t as good on the clips it cuts compared to clips you’d take in video mode. Even so, I think Magic Capture will be useful for parents trying to capture moments of their kids, without needing to work so hard to get the perfect smile for a photo. Instead of marketing this feature as something that lets you be in the moment by not looking at your phone at all, it would probably be better to pitch it as something that will automatically grab great photos and short video clips for you, and all you need to do is point your phone and hit record.
